* `std`'s `popcount`, `clz` and `ctz`, and `ffi`'s two copies
  (`src/runtime/runtime_ext.h`);
* libm, behind `math`;
* the graphics layer behind `gfx`, the ui layer behind `ui` and the PCM
  mixer behind `audio`, which are in the
  [goose_gfx](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_gfx) package;
* the physics layer behind `physics`, which is in the
  [goose_physics](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_physics) package.

Both packages are repositories of their own. The design and its rationale
are described in `design/stdlib_design.md` and in the packages' own
[docs/gfx.md](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_gfx/blob/main/docs/gfx.md),
[docs/ui.md](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_gfx/blob/main/docs/ui.md), [docs/audio.md](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_gfx/blob/main/docs/audio.md) and
[docs/physics.md](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_physics/blob/main/docs/physics.md).
This document is the reference.

For **text rendering, fonts and game HUDs**, start with
[`ui`](#text-rendering-and-game-huds), which renders over `gfx`. For external
binary file formats, use [`binary`](#binary); `from_bytes` reads Goose's own
serialization format. Text formats have modules of their own:
[`json`](#json), [`csv`](#csv) and [`base64`](#base64), and
[`regex`](#regex) searches text with regular expressions.

The library uses these conventions:

* A function that reads or mutates elements in place takes `xs: T[:]`; every
  array kind and every slice coerces to it: `sort(arr)`, `sort(arr[1..])`.
* A function that changes the length takes `xs: A&`, the whole array by
  reference, and instantiates for whatever array kind it is given, provided
  that kind has the operations used. A grow-only array shrinks through the
  reference wherever nothing in the caller points into it (spec §5.1), so
  `remove_at(xs, i)` works on a `[>..]` local; the checker rejects the
  call if a live reference or slice could be invalidated.
* Nothing non-fixed is taken by value (spec §4.1): `f(xs)` binds by
  reference, and a function that wants its own copy calls `copy(xs)`.
* Fresh arrays come back as `T[>..]`, built directly in the caller's
  destination: `let ys = filter(xs) { it > 0 };`, `out.append(map(xs) { … })`.
* "Maybe an element" is a `T?`: a reference into the input, or null for
  none. Narrow it with `if`/`guard`. Positions are `i64`, `-1` for none.
  Two-outcome scalars return a trailing `bool`: `let v, ok = parse_int(s);`.
* Blocks: `xs.find() { it > 3 }`, `sort(xs) { a, b => a.age < b.age }`. A
  comparator is always "a goes before b". Sorting, heap and extremum
  functions come with and without a block; without a block they compare
  with `<`.
* Text output goes into a `u8[>..]&` builder the caller passes; `str(…)` is
  the fresh-string form.
* UFCS applies: `xs.sort()`, `d.insert(k, v)`, `r.rand_int(6)`.
* A function taking an element *by value* (`push_n`, `insert_at`, `fill`,
  `heap_push`) cannot take one that contains self-relative references, because
  those values cannot be copied (spec §3.9). Construct them in place.
* The functions that move elements around (`swap_at`, `reverse`, `shuffle`,
  `sort`, `stable_sort`, `fill`, `copy_into`, `insert_at`, `remove_at`,
  `swap_remove`, `retain`, `dedup`, the heap functions) move the elements
  themselves, including references: `reverse(refs)` reorders an array of
  references and leaves what they point to unchanged, and an array of
  references to values that cannot be copied (spec §3.9) can be sorted too.
  They store whole elements with `.=`, as generic code may (spec §3.8). An
  array of relative references (self-relative or `in pool`) is reordered
  the same way. A `T` local or parameter holds the plain reference, and
  each element the reference is stored back into encodes it again. For a
  self-relative link, this requires the link to point within that
  element's root (spec §3.9), which a link moved within its own array does.
  `swap(a, b)` exchanges the values `a` and `b` refer to. `remove_at`,
  `swap_remove` and `heap_pop` return a copy of the removed value; for a
  reference element, they return a copy of its pointee. A reference element
  passed by value (`insert_at`, `heap_push`) is written `&x`, which makes
  `T` the reference type. `stable_sort` sorts an array of `in pool` links,
  but its temporary array cannot hold copies of self-relative links (spec
  §3.9).
* The `std`, `dictionary`, `slot_pool`, `slice_pool`, `vec`, `math`, and `os` names are global;
  `ffi`, `binary`, `base64`, `csv`, `json`, `regex`, `audio`, `gfx`,
  `physics`, `ui` and `exception` use their own namespaces, and so do the
  helpers `std` and `json` read and write float text with, in `float_text`.
  A local named `fill` or `count` shadows the global function of that name,
  so a call to that function is an error. A global variable of such a name does not
  shadow it, because the name in a call resolves past global variables to
  the functions (spec §11.1).
  Slice allocator implementation types and helpers use `slice_pool_detail`;
  applications should use the public pool operations.

title: Scalars and bits
text:
```goose
fn min<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T          fn max<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T
fn clamp<T>(x: T, lo: T, hi: T) -> T
fn abs<T>(x: T) -> T                // integers; abs(f32) and abs(f64) overloads
fn rem<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T         // integers; pairs with `/`
fn div_euclid<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T  // integers; pairs with `%`
fn sign<T>(x: T) -> T               // -1, 0, 1 at x's type; f32/f64 overloads
fn lerp(a: f64, b: f64, t: f64) -> f64      // and f32
fn next_pow2(x: i64) -> i64         // smallest power of two >= max(x, 1)
fn popcount(x: u64) -> i64
fn clz(x: u64) -> i64               // 64 for 0
fn ctz(x: u64) -> i64               // 64 for 0
fn swap<T>(a: T&, b: T&)            // swap(x, y)
```

`popcount`, `clz` and `ctz` are implemented in the runtime. Each is a single
instruction where the C compiler has one (MSVC's `popcount` needs
`/arch:AVX` or higher for that), and a loop under TinyCC.

`rem` is the remainder of truncating division: `rem(-7, 3) == -1`, paired
with `-7 / 3 == -2`. `div_euclid` is the quotient paired with Euclidean `%`:
`div_euclid(-7, 3) == -3` and `-7 % 3 == 2`. It rounds down for positive
divisors and up for negative ones (`div_euclid(-7, -3) == 3`). Thus a
coordinate's tile and offset are `div_euclid(x, width)` and `x % width`.

Both functions return the operands' integer type and abort on a zero
divisor. `rem(MIN, -1)` is zero, including at `i64`; `div_euclid` follows
`/`'s overflow rules (always abort at `i64.min, -1`; at narrower signed
widths, debug abort and release wrap). Unsigned `rem` and `div_euclid` are
ordinary `%` and `/`. Neither function takes floats; float `%` is already
the truncating remainder (`fmod`). The identities
`b * (a / b) + rem(a, b) == a` and
`b * div_euclid(a, b) + a % b == a` hold mathematically when the quotient
is representable, but evaluating their intermediate products can overflow.

title: Hashing
text:
```goose
fn hash(x: i8) -> u64               // ... one overload per integer type
fn hash(x: bool) -> u64             fn hash(x: f32) -> u64      fn hash(x: f64) -> u64
fn hash(s: u8[:]) -> u64            // 8 bytes per multiply; any u8 array coerces
fn hash_combine(seed: u64, h: u64) -> u64
```

These hashes mix all of their input into the low 32 bits. `dictionary`
masks those bits to find the home slot and keeps them as the slot's tag.
A float hashes as its bits, `-0.0` as `0.0`, and an `f32` as the `f64` of
its value.
`dictionary` also picks up a `hash` overload for a user key type, declared
globally or in the key type's namespace (it calls `key.hash()`, §11.1), and
that overload should do the same, as `hash_combine` of the fields' hashes
does:

```goose
struct key { a: i64, b: i64 }
fn hash(k: key) -> u64 { hash_combine(hash(k.a), hash(k.b)) }
```

title: Random numbers
text:
```goose
struct rng { s: u64 }                    // splitmix64; the seed is the state
fn rand_u64(r: rng&) -> u64
fn rand_int(r: rng&, n: i64) -> i64      // uniform in [0, n), without modulo bias; asserts n > 0
fn rand_flt(r: rng&) -> f64              // uniform in [0, 1)
fn shuffle<T>(xs: T[:], r: rng&)         // Fisher-Yates
```

```goose
var r = rng { os.random_seed() };   // or any fixed seed
let d = r.rand_int(6);
```

title: Arrays: reading and searching
text:
```goose
fn each_rev<T, F>(xs: T[:])                    // F(x), last to first
fn each_chunk<T, F>(xs: T[:], n: i64)          // F(chunk: T[:], i); the last chunk may be short
fn find<T, F>(xs: T[:]) -> T?                  // first x with F(x), as a reference
fn find_index<T, F>(xs: T[:]) -> i64
fn position<T>(xs: T[:], v: T) -> i64          // first i with xs[i] == v
fn contains<T>(xs: T[:], v: T) -> bool
fn any<T, F>(xs: T[:]) -> bool                 fn all<T, F>(xs: T[:]) -> bool
fn count<T, F>(xs: T[:]) -> i64                // number of x with F(x)
fn min<T>(xs: T[:]) -> T                       // asserts xs.len > 0; min(xs) { a, b => ... } too
fn max<T>(xs: T[:]) -> T
fn min_by<T, F>(xs: T[:]) -> i64               // index of the smallest F(x); -1 if empty
fn max_by<T, F>(xs: T[:]) -> i64
fn last<T>(xs: T[:]) -> T&                     // asserts xs.len > 0
fn lower_bound<T, F>(xs: T[:]) -> i64          // first i with !F(xs[i]); F true on a prefix
fn binary_search<T>(xs: T[:], v: T) -> i64, bool   // sorted by <: position (or insertion point), found
fn find<T>(xs: T[:], sub: T[:]) -> i64         // first occurrence of a subsequence, -1 if none
fn rfind<T>(xs: T[:], sub: T[:]) -> i64
fn starts_with<T>(xs: T[:], p: T[:]) -> bool   fn ends_with<T>(xs: T[:], p: T[:]) -> bool
```

`find`/`rfind`/`starts_with`/`ends_with` are generic over the element, so
they are the string functions too: `find(line, "://")`. `find` and `rfind`
compare a whole subsequence only where its first element matches.
(The function is named `position` rather than `index_of` because
`index_of` is the builtin that turns an element reference into its index.)

```goose
let big = xs.find() { it > 100 };
if big { print(big); }
var row = 0;
each_chunk(pixels, width) { line, y => row += line.len; };
```

title: Byte sets
Arrays: transforming
Arrays: in place
text:
```goose
fn fill<T>(xs: T[:], v: T)
fn copy_into<T>(dst: T[:], src: T[:])           // equal lengths; first to last
fn reverse<T>(xs: T[:])
fn sort<T>(xs: T[:])                            // by <; sort(xs) { a, b => ... } by the block
fn stable_sort<T>(xs: T[:])                     // natural merge sort; one temporary of xs.len elements
fn to_lower(s: u8[:])                           // ASCII, in place
fn to_upper(s: u8[:])
```

`copy_into` preserves its element-by-element, first-to-last semantics. For a
checked copy that preserves the source values when the slices overlap, use the
language operation `dst.move_from(src)` (fixed-size, copyable elements).

`sort` is a pattern-defeating quicksort based on pdqsort and Rust's
ipnsort. It is unstable (the order it leaves equal elements in is
unspecified), works in place and does not allocate. Its partition does not
branch on the comparisons, and a run of equal keys takes a linear pass
rather than n log n. Heapsort takes over a range that partitioning keeps
splitting badly, so the worst case is O(n log n).

`stable_sort` is a
natural merge sort: it finds the runs already in order (or in strictly
descending order, which it reverses) and merges them pass by pass between
`xs` and a temporary of `xs.len` elements on a fresh data stack.

Both make a
single pass over input that is already in order or strictly descending,
and neither allocates for such input or for 20 elements or fewer. A
comparator that is not a strict weak ordering (`<=`, or `<` over floats
with NaNs) leaves the elements in an unspecified order, but the result is
always a permutation of the input, and neither function aborts.

A `let` array can be sorted because `let` prevents rebinding, not element
writes. A `const` array or read-only slice cannot be sorted (spec §9.5).

title: Arrays: changing the length
text:
```goose
fn push_n<A, T>(xs: A&, v: T, n: i64)           // n pushes
fn insert_at<A, T>(xs: A&, i: i64, v: T)        // shifts [i..) up; needs push
fn remove_at<A>(xs: A&, i: i64) -> T            // shifts down; needs pop
fn swap_remove<A>(xs: A&, i: i64) -> T          // O(1), reorders
fn retain<A, F>(xs: A&)                         // keeps x with F(x), in order; needs resize
fn dedup<A>(xs: A&)                             // drops adjacent duplicates
fn heap_push<A, T>(xs: A&, v: T)                // min-heap by <; block forms of all three
fn heap_pop<A>(xs: A&) -> T
fn make_heap<A>(xs: A&)                         // O(n)
```

A `[>..<]` is the natural heap and queue container; a limited `[..k]` field
works as well.

The heap is binary, with the children of `i` at `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`. Its
sifts move a hole instead of swapping elements. The element being placed
waits in a local while each level moves one element into the hole, and it
is stored once, where the hole stops. `heap_pop` walks the hole from the
root down to a leaf, along the child that goes first, and then sifts the
last element up from there, as libstdc++ and Rust do. This takes about one
comparison per level, where sifting the element down from the root takes
two. For a comparator that is a strict weak order, every operation leaves
the same layout as the textbook swapping sifts, including for ties, so
elements that tie come out in the same order. A comparator that reads the
heap while it runs sees one slot holding a copy of its neighbour rather
than the element waiting outside.

```goose
var q: i64[>..<] = [];
q.heap_push(5); q.heap_push(1);
let smallest = q.heap_pop();
```

title: Strings
text:
```goose
fn format_int<B>(out: B&, v: i64, base: i64, width: i64, padc: u8)   // base 2..36, right-aligned
fn format_uint<B>(out: B&, v: u64, base: i64, width: i64, padc: u8)   // B: u8[>..] or u8[..k]
fn format_flt(out: u8[>..]&, v: f64, decimals: i64)        // fixed decimals, the exact value rounded half up; inf/-inf/nan as print writes them
fn parse_int(s: u8[:], base: i64 = 10) -> i64, bool        // optional sign, whole string; false outside i64
fn parse_flt(s: u8[:]) -> f64, bool                        // sign, fraction, exponent; correctly rounded
fn format_uleb(out: u8[>..]&, v: i64)                     // LEB128 (3.6), 1-10 bytes
fn parse_uleb(s: u8[:]) -> i64, i64                       // value and byte count; 0, 0 if malformed
fn compare(a: u8[:], b: u8[:]) -> i64                      // bytewise: -1, 0, 1
fn trim(s: u8[:]) -> u8[:]                                 // ASCII whitespace; a sub-slice
fn trim_start(s: u8[:]) -> u8[:]                           fn trim_end(s: u8[:]) -> u8[:]
fn split(s: u8[:], sep: u8) -> const u8[:][>..]            // read-only slices into s; empty parts kept
fn split(s: u8[:], sep: u8[:]) -> const u8[:][>..]         // matched from the left; an empty sep: [s]
fn each_split<F>(s: u8[:], sep: u8)                        // F(part); no array built
fn each_split<F>(s: u8[:], sep: u8[:])
fn words(s: u8[:]) -> const u8[:][>..]                     // split at runs of ASCII whitespace; no empty words
fn each_word<F>(s: u8[:])                                  // F(word)
fn join<T>(out: u8[>..]&, parts: T[:], sep: u8[:])         // T any u8 array/slice type
fn format_replaced(out: u8[>..]&, s: u8[:], old: u8[:], with: u8[:])
fn each_utf8<F>(s: u8[:])                                  // F(codepoint); malformed bytes give 0xFFFD
fn push_utf8(out: u8[>..]&, cp: i64)                       // 0xFFFD's bytes for cp outside 0..0x10FFFF
```

The builtins `format`/`str`/`print` do the plain rendering of scalars and
strings; the functions here add control over the output, and parsing. In
base 10, `format_int` and `format_uint` write the same text as `format`
(after any padding) and run as fast. `parse_flt` gives the double nearest to
the decimal, as C's `strtod` does, so a float's text from `print` or
`format` reads back as the same value. Strings are `u8` arrays: input is a
`u8[:]`, output goes to a `u8[>..]&` builder, and storage is a `u8[]` or
`u8[..k]`.

`each_utf8` decodes as the WHATWG decoder does. A sequence cut short, an
overlong form, a surrogate or a code point past 0x10FFFF gives one 0xFFFD
for each maximal subpart (Unicode §3.9), and the byte that broke a sequence
starts the next one: `[0xC3, 'A']` gives 0xFFFD and then `A`. `push_utf8`
writes a surrogate as the three bytes of its own code, which is how `json`
keeps a lone `\u` escape.

```goose
var line: u8[>..] = [];
format(line, "x=");
format_int(line, x, 16, 8, '0');
each_split(text, '\n') { handle(trim(it)); };
let n, ok = parse_int(trim(field));
let cmd = words(input);                   // "take  the sword": ["take", "the", "sword"]
if cmd.len > 1 && cmd[0] == "take" { take(cmd[cmd.len - 1]); }
```

`format_uleb` and `parse_uleb` write and read the length prefix used by
serialized images (`design/serialization.md`). Writing the prefix separately
lets a program save a `bytes_of` view without first copying it into an image.
Reading the prefix tells a stream reader how many payload bytes to expect.

```goose
let payload = pool.bytes_of();            // a view, nothing copied
var head: u8[>..] = [];
format_uleb(head, payload.len);
write_file(path, head); append_file(path, payload);
```

`format_flt` rounds the exact binary value of `v`, at any size and to any
number of places: `format_flt(out, 0.1, 20)` writes
`0.10000000000000000555`, as C's `printf("%.20f")` does, and
`format_flt(out, 2.675, 2)` writes `2.67`, since the double nearest 2.675
is just below it. Only a value that is exactly halfway rounds differently
from `printf`, which rounds half to even: `format_flt(out, 0.125, 2)`
writes `0.13`. The plain `format` writes the shortest text that reads back
as the same value.

title: exception
text:
Typed exceptions implemented in Goose with `return ... from` (spec §7.9),
inspired by [Lobster's exception module](https://github.com/aardappel/lobster/blob/master/modules/exception.lobster).
Import `exception`; its functions are in namespace `exception`.

```goose
fn try<E, Body, Catch>()            // Body(); on an error, Catch(error)
fn try<E, Body>()                   // Body(); discard an error
fn try<E, Body, Catch, Finally>()   // as the first, then Finally() on every way out
fn throw(value)                    // exit the nearest enclosing handler
```

```goose
import exception;

fn load() {
    // This can be any number of calls below try.
    exception::throw(str("cannot load item ", 42));
}

exception::try<u8[]>(load) { error => print(error); };
```

`E` is the error type, supplied explicitly at `try`: `u8[]` for owned text,
an integer, or an application's struct or enum (`Error..` for a
variable-mode enum). The thrown value must fit `E`, which must be usable
as an array element. The body and catch are static function values;
Goose permits one trailing block, so name at least one of the callbacks.
The body's results are discarded; it can update captured output variables.

The handler returns an empty `E[]` on success and a singleton containing
the error on failure. This uses the ordinary data stacks, needs no default
`E`, and allows `0`, `false`, and `""` as errors. The catch runs after that
handler has returned. Calling `throw` in the catch therefore throws to an
outer `try`; use `exception::throw(copy(error))` to rethrow an owned
variable-size error. An existing non-fixed value likewise needs `copy`
when first thrown; fresh constructors and string slices can be supplied
directly. Owned text is copied before the frames containing it exit.

The language's checks and limitations still apply:

* Every throw must have a handler on every compile-time call path, including
  throws from a catch. An incompatible error type is a compile error.
* References carried by a long-distance return must point to globals or
  static data. Use owned `u8[]`, not a slice into a local string, and owned
  fields in error records.
* Recursive code can throw to an outer handler. A `try` cannot itself be
  re-entered recursively: its non-fixed handler result would hold a data
  stack across the recursive call (§7.8).
* The checker propagates calls that never resume their caller. A function
  declared to return a value may end with `exception::throw(error);`, and a
  throwing branch needs no result. This does not give `throw` a value type:
  use it as a statement or branch, rather than `return throw(error);` or as
  an argument that requires a value. Recursive inference is conservative
  (spec §7.3).
* Only calls to `throw` are caught. Runtime failures, `abort` and `exit`
  remain uncatchable. There is no stack-trace facility.

`try<E>(body, catch, finally)` runs `finally` after the body completes, after
a caught throw, and when a throw or a lexical `return` aimed at another
function leaves through the call. It is `defer finally();` ahead of the try
(reference, "defer"), so `finally` follows the rules of a defer body: it
cannot leave, and it may not throw, catch, or call anything that does.

title: dictionary
text:
```goose
struct dictionary<K, V> { count: i64, slots: dictionary_slot<K, V>[>..<] }
fn get<K, V>(d: dictionary<K, V>&, key: K) -> V?               // reference to the value, or null
fn contains<K, V>(d: dictionary<K, V>&, key: K) -> bool
fn insert<K, V>(d: dictionary<K, V>&, key: K, val: V) -> bool   // overwrites; true if new
fn get_or_insert<K, V>(d: dictionary<K, V>&, key: K, v0: V) -> V&
fn update<K, V, F>(d: dictionary<K, V>&, key: K, v0: V)         // F(val&); inserts v0 first if absent
fn remove<K, V>(d: dictionary<K, V>&, key: K) -> bool
fn clear<K, V>(d: dictionary<K, V>&)
fn reserve<K, V>(d: dictionary<K, V>&, n: i64)                  // room for n entries without a rehash
fn each<K, V, F>(d: dictionary<K, V>&)                          // F(key, val&); order unspecified
```

The table uses open addressing with linear probing, a power-of-two capacity
and backward-shift deletion. Keys and values are fixed-size; a key type
needs `hash` and `==`. Each slot keeps 31 bits of its key's hash as a tag,
so a lookup compares keys only where the tags agree, and growth and removal
do not hash keys again (in tables of up to 2^31 slots). `insert`, `update`
and `get_or_insert` look a key up once, whether or not it is there. The
table doubles in place at 2/3 load; `reserve(n)` sizes it for `n` entries
at that load.
Strings are keyed as `u8[:]` slices into text the caller keeps (`const u8[:]`
for literals or views of `const` data, §9.5), or as inline
`u8[..k]`. A set is `dictionary<K, bool>`.

The slot array is grow-shrink, so a reference into it (a `get` or
`get_or_insert` result, or an `each` binder) must have its last use before
the next `insert`, `update`, `remove` or `clear`. Otherwise the checker
reports an error at the mutation, naming the reference and where it was
bound (spec §5.2). Finish with the reference first, or use `update`, which
does the lookup and the change in one call:

```goose
var counts = dictionary<const u8[:], i32> {};
each_split(text, ' ') { counts.update(it, 0) { it += 1; } };
counts.each() { w, n => if n > 100 { print(w, " ", n); } };
let n = counts.get("the");
if n { print(n); }               // the last use of n; counts is free again after it
```

The checker looks at liveness, not scope: a reference whose last use comes
before the mutation needs no block around it, and a reference still used
after the mutation is an error wherever it was declared. The key type is
`const u8[:]` because literals and the read-only views returned by `split`
require it (§9.5). A dictionary holding writable slices can use
`dictionary<u8[:], V>`, whether the underlying buffer is bound with `let`
or `var`.

A value can be a reference if it is optional: `Cell?`, or a link into a
pool such as `Cell&<u32 in cells>?`. The unused slots hold `default<V>()`,
which a non-optional reference does not have. `insert` over an existing key
stores the new reference rather than writing through the old one. `get` and
`get_or_insert` return the stored reference itself, and the blocks of
`update` and `each` receive it (`V?` and `V&` of a reference are that
reference, §3.8), loaded if it is relative. Writing through it writes the
pointee; replacing it requires an `insert`. `get` returns null both for a
null value and for an absent key; `contains` tells them apart. Such a
reference points at its pointee rather than into the slot array, so it may
stay live across the next mutation:

```goose
var owner = dictionary<i64, Cell?> {};
owner.insert(7, cells[3]);
let c = owner.get(7);
owner.insert(7, cells[4]);       // cells[3] is unchanged, and c still refers to it
if c { c.v += 1; }
```

title: Migrating from reusable
text:
`reusable` and `reusable[]` are deprecated; their builtins are still available.
Import `slot_pool` for individual slots or `slice_pool` for contiguous runs.

| Existing spelling | Library spelling |
|---|---|
| `reusable var p: T[>..] = [];` | `var p = slot_pool<T> {};` |
| `reusable[] var p: T[>..] = [];` | `var p = slice_pool<T> {};` |
| pool parameter `p: T[>..]&` | `p: slot_pool<T>&` or `p: slice_pool<T>&` |
| `p[i]`, `p.len`, `for x in p` | `p.items[i]`, `p.items.len`, `for x in p.items` |
| `u32 in p`, `Node&<u32 in p>` | `u32 in p.items`, `Node&<u32 in p.items>` |
| `p.alloc_ref(value)` | same for copyable values; `p.alloc_with() { fresh_value }` for in-place construction |
| `p.alloc_index(value)` | same for copyable values; `p.alloc_index_with() { fresh_value }` for in-place construction |
| `p.free(i)` | same; or `p.free_ref(node)` when the element is not itself a reference |
| `p.alloc_slice(n)`, `p.free_slice(s)`, `p.realloc_slice(s, n)` | same method spellings on `slice_pool` |
| allocate a slice, then copy into it | `p.alloc_copy(source)` |

Both libraries keep stable, initialized backing storage. `items.len` is the
high-water count, including free entries, and iteration visits those entries.
Freed references/views remain valid and can observe replacement values; logical
use-after-free and double-free detection require application bookkeeping.
`recycle_all` makes all storage reusable without shrinking it or clearing values.
Do not shrink/replace `items` or modify allocator bookkeeping directly.

Wrong-pool slot frees through `free_ref` retain `index_of`'s compile-time check.
Wrong-pool nonempty slice frees currently fail a runtime containment check
(`slice_pool.free_slice: slice is not from this pool`); there is no
compile-time warning yet. Empty slices from any origin are harmless. Like
every check inside the standard library, the pools' report the line of the
program that called them.
Eligible `items` can be serialized independently, but this omits allocator state.
Whole root owners cannot be serialized or copied to workers automatically.
For flat elements, [the worker snapshot sample](../samples/32_pool_worker_snapshots.goose)
copies `items` and allocator metadata explicitly into a worker-local owner.
Its slice metadata types are implementation details, so keep that recipe in step
with the library rather than treating it as a stable serialization format.

Pool references can be stored in ordinary structs, captured, returned while their
owner lives, and made optional. This is more flexible than builtin pool references.
The owning root itself remains local/global-only; nested owning roots are deferred.

title: slot_pool
text:
`import slot_pool;` provides stable, reusable slots through ordinary root-struct
fields and functions. Use it instead of the deprecated `reusable` language feature.

```goose
root struct slot_pool<T> {
    items: T[>..] = [],
    free_slots: i64[>..<] = []
}

fn alloc_index<T>(pool: slot_pool<T>&, value: T) -> i64
fn alloc_ref<T>(pool: slot_pool<T>&, value: T) -> T&
fn alloc_with<T, F>(pool: slot_pool<T>&) -> T&
fn alloc_index_with<T, F>(pool: slot_pool<T>&) -> i64
fn free<T>(pool: slot_pool<T>&, i: i64)
fn free_ref<T>(pool: slot_pool<T>&, value: T&)
fn recycle_all<T>(pool: slot_pool<T>&)
```

Declare a local or global owner and use `items` for ordinary indexing, slicing,
iteration and `index_of`:

```goose
import slot_pool;

fn main() {
    var pool = slot_pool<i64> {};
    let first .= pool.alloc_ref(10);
    let index = pool.items.index_of(first);
    pool.free(index);
    assert(pool.alloc_index(20) == index);
    print(first);                         // 20: the same slot, now reused
}
```

Elements must be fixed-size. No default value is needed: every allocation
supplies a value. `alloc_index` and `alloc_ref` take normally copyable values.
An allocation takes the most recently
freed index, or appends when no slot is free. `alloc_index` returns its index;
`alloc_ref` returns a reference to its value. For reference elements, `T&`
collapses to `T` as usual; use `alloc_index` when the slot's identity is needed.
Whole-element assignment replaces reference-valued elements without writing
through them.

`alloc_with` and `alloc_index_with` take a zero-argument function or trailing block
producing `T`; the latter returns the chosen index directly.
It selects the slot first, calls the builder once, and constructs the result
directly there. This supports self-relative links and pool-relative `self`:

```goose
import slot_pool;
struct Node { value: i64, me: Node&<u32>, next: Node&<u32>? }
fn main() {
    var nodes = slot_pool<Node> {};
    let first .= nodes.alloc_with() { Node { value: 1, me: self } };
    let second .= nodes.alloc_with() { Node { value: 2, me: self, next: first } };
    let index = nodes.items.index_of(second);
    nodes.free(index);
    nodes.alloc_with() { Node { value: 3, me: self, next: first } };
    assert(second.value == 3 && second.me .== second);
}
```

Fresh results may come from other functions. Existing self-relative values
still cannot be copied, and links must point within the receiving array.
A trailing block infers its result type; for a reference-valued `T`, pass a
named function explicitly returning that reference type.

Unlike value arguments, the builder runs after a free index has been removed.
A slot freed by the builder stays available for a later allocation. A fresh
slot joins `items.len` only when construction completes; a nonlocal return
before completion does not publish it. Reuse is not transactional: a nonlocal
exit does not restore the popped index or undo initializer side effects.
The usual construction rules reject conflicting growth of `items` during
the builder. Bounds checks on a recycled index run before the builder.

`free` checks `0 <= i < items.len` in every build, then records the index. It
leaves the element initialized and does not shrink the array. Existing references
remain valid and can observe a later replacement. Double frees and use of a
logically freed slot are application errors, as with `reusable`; the pool does
not track occupancy or generations. `items.len` is the number of slots ever
appended, including free ones, and iteration visits those slots too.

Treat `free_slots` as bookkeeping. Do not shrink or replace `items`, or edit the
freelist directly: doing so can invalidate the pool's logical state. Ordinary
array bounds and lifetime checks still apply. `recycle_all` makes every slot
available again in index order, retaining initialized values and backing storage.
It does not shrink `items`, destroy values, or invalidate existing references.
`free_ref` combines `index_of` with `free`, retaining its compile-time provenance
check; use indices for reference-valued elements, whose references name the
pointee rather than the pool slot. An eligible `items` component
can be serialized separately, but its image omits the freelist.

For a global `var pool`, compact links and index types can name its array:
`Node&<u32 in pool.items>`, `u32 in pool.items`, and `u32 upto pool.items`.
Pool-relative values with ordinary links are copyable and work with `alloc_ref`.
Self-relative values and `self` initializers use `alloc_with` to construct at
the allocated slot.
A root owner cannot be copied to a worker; worker-local pools are allowed.
See [the migration plan](design/root_structs.md#separate-follow-up-reusable-pools-in-the-stdlib).

title: slice_pool
text:
`import slice_pool;` provides reusable contiguous runs of fixed-size elements.
`alloc_slice` and `realloc_slice` require defaults; `alloc_copy` only requires
copyable values. An owner is declared as `var pool = slice_pool<T> {};`.
Use it instead of the deprecated `reusable[]` language feature. Both builtins
remain available for existing code; their removal is a separate future step.

```goose
fn alloc_slice<T>(pool: slice_pool<T>&, n: i64) -> T[:]
fn alloc_copy<T>(pool: slice_pool<T>&, src: T[:]) -> T[:]
fn free_slice<T>(pool: slice_pool<T>&, s: T[:])
fn realloc_slice<T>(pool: slice_pool<T>&, s: T[:], n: i64) -> T[:]
fn recycle_all<T>(pool: slice_pool<T>&)
```

```goose
import slice_pool;
fn main() {
    var pool = slice_pool<i64> {};
    var entries = pool.alloc_slice(3);
    entries[0] = 7;
    entries = pool.realloc_slice(entries, 5);
    print(entries);                         // [7, 0, 0, 0, 0]
    pool.free_slice(entries);
    let again = pool.alloc_slice(2);
    print(again, " ", pool.items.len);       // [0, 0] 5
}
```

Allocation selects the first free span in index order that fits. If none fits,
it grows the backing array, using any free span at the tail first. Free spans
coalesce with their neighbors. An augmented B+ tree of 512-byte nodes handles
first-fit search and neighbor lookup with tree walks and bounded node scans;
emptied nodes are reused. The tree code is the runtime's, `reusable[]`'s, in a
copy that checks what it reads from `nodes` and `tree`, so the policy matches.

`alloc_slice` defaults every element it hands out, including reused elements.
`alloc_copy` initializes directly from a source slice, without default-filling
first. It supports overlapping views of `items` and does not free the source.
For example, `strings.alloc_copy(text)` allocates and copies a string.
`realloc_slice` preserves the first `min(s.len, n)` elements, returns a shortened
tail to the tree, and defaults each added element once. Growth stays in place
at the array's end or when the following free span suffices (including tail
extension). Otherwise it frees the old run and selects the first fit, copying
with overlap-safe ordering. Default expressions must not mutate or reenter the
same pool. Every published backing-array element is initialized.

`free_slice` and `realloc_slice` accept subranges of a pool run. They check that
a nonempty slice is aligned and wholly within `items`, even when its origin is
only known at runtime. Empty/default slices can be freed harmlessly; growing an
empty slice allocates a new run. Negative or oversized counts abort in every
build before the tree changes. `items.range_index(s)` recovers a nonempty run's
index; it returns zero for every empty slice.

Freeing and shrinking runs do not shrink `items` or invalidate old views. A
retained view observes later replacements at its original address; relocation
does not retarget it. Double frees, overlapping live allocations caused by
invalid frees, and accessing a logically freed run are application errors.
`items.len` is the high-water length, not the count of live elements. Treat
`nodes` and `tree` as internal bookkeeping, and do not shrink or replace `items`.
Ordinary bounds and lifetime checks still apply to these public fields. The
runtime checks every node number and entry count it reads from them: one a
program wrote wrong aborts with `slice pool span tree is corrupt`. A span
edited to start past `items` aborts with `span tree is corrupt` from the
operation that drew it; other edited spans can hand elements out twice, as a
double free can.
`recycle_all` makes the entire high-water range one free run and recycles all
metadata nodes. It retains initialized values, backing storage and existing
views; the next allocation starts at index zero.

The owner follows the same placement, serialization and worker restrictions as
`slot_pool`: serialize eligible `items` separately, and construct worker-local
owners rather than transferring root owners. `alloc_slice` constructs defaults
in place, so allocation and free support defaultable self-relative elements;
`realloc_slice` requires normally copyable elements, just as the builtin does.
Global index/pool-relative types can name `pool.items`, as for `slot_pool`.
Optional references to separately owned storage and declared field defaults are
supported when `T` has a default.

See the [slice-pool benchmark report](../bench/slice_pool.md) for comparisons
against `reusable[]`, including preserved function-call boundaries.

title: vec
text:
```goose
struct vec2<T> { x: T, y: T }       struct vec3<T> { x: T, y: T, z: T }
struct vec4<T> { x: T, y: T, z: T, w: T }
type float2/float3/float4 = vec*<f32>   double2/3/4 = vec*<f64>   int2/3/4 = vec*<i32>
let float3_0 = float3 { 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 };  // _0 and _1 for all nine aliases

fn dot<T>(a: vec3<T>, b: vec3<T>) -> T          // all sizes
fn cross<T>(a: vec3<T>, b: vec3<T>) -> vec3<T>
fn length_sq<T>(v: vec3<T>) -> T
fn length<T>(v: vec3<T>) -> T                   // float vectors
fn normalize<T>(v: vec3<T>) -> vec3<T>
fn distance<T>(a: vec3<T>, b: vec3<T>) -> T
fn lerp<T>(a: vec3<T>, b: vec3<T>, t: T) -> vec3<T>
fn xy<T>(v: vec3<T>) -> vec2<T>                 // also xy(vec4), xyz(vec4)
```

Elementwise `+ - * /` are built into the language (`a + b`, `p - q`), and
so is unary minus on a float or signed integer vector (`-v`). `*` and `/`
also broadcast a scalar in either order: `v * 2.0`, `v / length(v)`,
`1.0 / v`; `v *= scale` and `v /= scale` update a vector in place. The
scalar converts to the component type, so an `f64` variable scaling a
`float3` needs an explicit `as f32`. Per-component
`min`/`max` is written out (`min(a.x, b.x)`).

title: math
text:
`math` provides libm at both widths (`sin(x)` picks `sin` or `sinf` by the
argument's type): `sqrt sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 exp log log2 log10
pow floor ceil round trunc`. These return floats as C does (`as i64`
converts).
`sqrt` is implemented in the runtime (`gs_sqrt`, `gs_sqrtf`). It gives the
same correctly rounded root as C, and NaN below zero, but without C's
errno, so it is the bare square root instruction where the C compiler
allows. The other functions for which C sets errno (`sin` to `pow`) are
libm's own functions under runtime names (`gs_exp`, `gs_expf`, ...), which
gcc and clang are told depend only on their arguments. Since Goose has no
errno, a call does not make the C compiler reload values that a loop
around the call holds in registers. An integer argument converts to both
widths equally well, so the call has to name one (`sqrt(n as f64)`);
`sqrt(n * 0.5)` calls the `f64` version, as `sqrt(0.5)` does.

`mul_add(x, y, z)`, at both widths, is `x * y + z` rounded once where the
code is built for FMA and twice where it is not. Which one a call gets is
up to the implementation (spec §7.12). The C backend rounds once on arm64,
on x86-64 built for AVX2 or later (`-march=x86-64-v3`, clang-cl's
`/arch:AVX2`), and in a `simd fn`'s AVX2 and AVX-512 versions. It rounds
twice elsewhere, under MSVC and under the JIT. `x * y + z` written out always rounds twice.

The two roundings can give very different results, not just a different
last bit:

- **Cancellation.** Where `x * y` and `z` nearly cancel, the fused result
  keeps the product's low bits and the unfused one loses them, so one can
  be zero where the other isn't. `mul_add(x, x, -(1.0 + 2.0 * (x - 1.0)))`
  with `x = 1 + 2^-30` is `2^-60` fused and `0.0` unfused, and a branch on
  it goes either way.
- **Overflow.** `mul_add(1.0e308, 2.0, -1.0e308)` is `1.0e308` fused, but
  `inf` unfused, because the product overflows before the add.

Inside a `simd fn`, only the calls Goose emits in that function's own body
fuse: its own code, and the functions Goose inlines into it. A call in a
plain helper that the `simd fn` calls keeps the helper's rounding, even if
the C compiler inlines the helper later. Whether Goose inlines a small
helper depends on the optimization level, so moving a `mul_add` into a
helper can change both the result and the speed between `-O0` and `-O2`.
Marking the helper `inline fn` keeps its calls fused in `simd` callers at
every level except `-O0`, where Goose inlines nothing. A function value is resolved at compile time, so a `simd fn`
given `mul_add` as one (`F(x, y, z)` with `F` = `mul_add`) fuses like a
direct call.

The module also has:

```goose
let PI = 3.141592653589793;   let TAU = 6.283185307179586;
fn radians(deg: f64) -> f64   fn degrees(rad: f64) -> f64      // and f32
fn is_nan(x: f64) -> bool     fn is_inf(x: f64) -> bool        // and f32
fn is_finite(x: f64) -> bool                                   // not inf or NaN; and f32
```

title: os
text:
A small interface to `src/runtime/runtime_os.h`:

```goose
fn read_file(path: const u8[:], out: u8[>..]&) -> bool     // appends the whole file
fn write_file(path: const u8[:], data: const u8[:]) -> bool
fn write_file_atomic(path: const u8[:], data: const u8[:]) -> bool   // the old file or all of the new
fn append_file(path: const u8[:], data: const u8[:]) -> bool
fn file_exists(path: const u8[:]) -> bool                  // a file, not a directory
fn delete_file(path: const u8[:]) -> bool
fn rename_file(from: const u8[:], to: const u8[:]) -> bool // replaces `to` atomically
fn make_dir(path: const u8[:]) -> bool                     // true if one is there afterwards
fn is_dir(path: const u8[:]) -> bool
fn delete_dir(path: const u8[:]) -> bool                   // an empty one
fn list_dir(path: const u8[:], out: u8[>..]&) -> bool      // appends each name and '\n', sorted
fn read_line(out: u8[>..]&) -> bool                  // stdin, newline stripped; false at end
fn read_stdin(out: u8[>..]&)                         // everything until end of input
fn write_stdout(s: const u8[:])   fn write_stderr(s: const u8[:])   fn flush_stdout()
fn arg_count() -> i64       fn arg(i: i64, out: u8[>..]&)
fn args() -> u8[:][>..]                              // indexable; argument 0 is the program
fn env(name: const u8[:], out: u8[>..]&) -> bool
fn trim_memory() -> bool                            // return unused data-stack pages to the OS
fn resource_dir() -> u8[>..]                         // absolute directory, trailing separator
fn resource_dir(out: u8[>..]&) -> bool               // appends; unchanged on failure
fn time() -> f64                                     // seconds since the epoch
fn clock() -> f64                                    // monotonic, high resolution
fn time_ns() -> i64         fn clock_ns() -> i64
fn sleep(seconds: f64)      fn sleep_ms(ms: i64)
fn random_seed() -> u64                              // entropy, for rng
```

`trim_memory` asks the OS to discard complete pages beyond every current
data-stack top in the calling thread program, including its globals and
scratch from scopes that have ended. It preserves live values, borrowed
views, limited-array capacity and virtual-address reservations; subsequent
growth works normally. It affects no other worker. Use it after a large
workload, such as replacing a document, rather than after every temporary
value. Ordinary scope exit keeps pages available for cheap reuse, while a
trimmed page causes a page fault when the stack grows into it again.

The pages are released immediately. Windows decommits them, which also
returns their commit charge, and Linux drops them from the resident set
at once. macOS replaces the unused suffix of each reservation with fresh
anonymous memory at the same addresses. On all three platforms, a stack
that grows again gets fresh zeroed pages. macOS trimming covers the full
unused reservation so ordinary growth needs no runtime tracking or signal
handling. `false` means at least one OS request failed.

Paths are UTF-8 on every platform; on Windows the runtime converts them to
UTF-16 for the system's wide APIs. Environment values and the program's
arguments are UTF-8 too. On Windows the arguments pass through the ANSI
code page first, so they keep only the characters that code page has. A
path is refused, and the call returns `false`, if it is longer than 4095
bytes, contains a NUL byte, or (on Windows) is not valid UTF-8, because a
path that was cut short or decoded another way could name a different
file.

`read_file` appends nothing when it fails. `read_stdin` appends the bytes
unchanged, on Windows too, where the C library's text mode would turn each
`\r\n` into a `\n` and stop at a Ctrl-Z. `read_line` strips a `\r` before a
line's newline, along with the newline.

`write_file_atomic` is for files that must never be seen half-written, such
as saved games. It writes the data to a new file in the same directory as
`path`, named after `path` with a random tag and `.tmp` added. It then
flushes that file to disk and renames it over `path`, keeping the
permissions of `path` on POSIX. A crash or a failure at any point leaves
`path` with either its old contents or all of the new ones. On a failure
the new file is removed; after a crash it can remain, with a name ending in
`.tmp`.
`rename_file` does the same one-step replacement for a file the program
wrote itself, within one volume. On Windows, a file cannot be replaced
while another program has it open, and virus scanners briefly open files
that were just written, so both functions wait up to about a second for
such a file before returning `false`.

`list_dir` leaves out `.` and `..` and sorts the names bytewise, so a
listing does not depend on the file system. A name that cannot be written
as one line of UTF-8 (a POSIX name containing a newline, or a Windows name
that is not valid UTF-16) is left out too. On a failure nothing is
appended.

```goose
var names: u8[>..] = [];
if list_dir("saves", names) {
    each_split(names, '\n') { if it.len > 0 { load_save(str("saves/", it)); } };
}
if !write_file_atomic("saves/slot1.sav", image) { write_stderr("not saved\n"); }
```

title: Application resources
text:
Ordinary relative paths resolve against the process working directory, as
in C/C++. Goose does not change that directory when it starts a program.
For data distributed with the application, `resource_dir()` returns an
absolute UTF-8 directory with a trailing separator, ready to concatenate:

```goose
var wad: u8[>..] = [];
if !read_file(str(resource_dir(), "data/map.wad"), wad) {
    abort("cannot read map.wad");
}
```

In JIT runs the root is the entry source's directory, regardless of which
imported module calls the helper. In AOT programs it is the running
executable's directory, discovered at runtime rather than recorded at
compilation. In a conventional macOS `.app` bundle it is `Contents/Resources/`.
Deploy the data relative to that root; moving the executable and its data
together preserves resource lookup. An AOT program does not depend on its
original source tree or on the launcher's working directory. A shared
library that an `extern "..." { }` block names with a path separator, such
as `"bin/steam_api64"`, is opened relative to the same root (spec §7.10),
so a library shipped beside the program is found the same way as its data.

The string-returning form aborts if the directory cannot be discovered;
the builder overload returns false and appends nothing. Native discovery
supports Windows, Linux and macOS. This directory is for shipped assets;
it is not guaranteed to be writable. User-supplied paths, outputs and saves
can continue to use ordinary file operations and their chosen locations.

`exit(code)` and `abort(msg)` are builtins, so that the checker knows they
diverge. Subprocesses and networking are not in v1; they arrive as
`extern fn`s when a program needs them.

title: ffi
text:
```goose
fn cstr(p: u64, out: u8[>..]&) -> bool       // the C string at p, its NUL left out; false for null
fn cstr(p: u64) -> u8[>..]                   // the same, fresh; empty for null
fn bytes(p: u64, n: i64, out: u8[>..]&) -> bool   // the n bytes at p; false for null
fn bytes(p: u64, n: i64) -> u8[>..]
```

These functions read memory that a C library owns. A function bound from a
shared library
(spec §7.10, [reference.md §24](reference.md#24-calling-c-and-being-called-from-c))
returns a `const char *`, or an array that the library keeps, as a `u64`,
which Goose cannot read through. These functions copy the data into Goose
storage, so foreign memory never becomes a Goose value without a copy.
They trust the pointer and the length, as every extern call trusts C: a
wrong pointer or length is the same kind of error as in C, and it is not
caught. A null pointer appends nothing and gives the `false` result.

```goose
import ffi;
extern "SDL2" {
    fn SDL_Init(flags: u32) -> i32;
    fn SDL_GetError() -> u64;
}
if SDL_Init(0x20) < 0 { abort(str("SDL: ", ffi::cstr(SDL_GetError()))); }
```

title: binary
text:
Checked reads of external formats, little- and big-endian, written in Goose
(floats take their bits through one small runtime helper).
`import binary;` puts the API in namespace `binary`. Input is a `const u8[:]`;
returned byte slices and fixed-width names borrow that input without copying
or allocating. Their lifetimes and read-only access are checked normally.
This API does not interpret Goose serialization images (`from_bytes`).

title: Reads at offsets
text:
```goose
fn range_ok(data: const u8[:], at: i64, size: i64) -> bool
fn read_u8(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> u8, bool
fn read_i8(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> i8, bool
fn read_u16le(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> u16, bool    // and read_u16be
fn read_i16le(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> i16, bool    // and read_i16be
fn read_u32le(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> u32, bool    // and read_u32be
fn read_i32le(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> i32, bool    // and read_i32be
fn read_u64le(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> u64, bool    // and read_u64be
fn read_i64le(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> i64, bool    // and read_i64be
fn read_f32le(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> f32, bool    // and read_f32be
fn read_f64le(data: const u8[:], at: i64) -> f64, bool    // and read_f64be
fn read_bytes(data: const u8[:], at: i64, size: i64) -> const u8[:], bool
fn read_name(data: const u8[:], at: i64, width: i64) -> const u8[:], bool
```

Offsets and sizes are bytes. Negative values, truncated fields and offsets
past the end fail with zero or an empty slice and `false`; range checking
does not overflow on extreme offsets or sizes. An empty range at the end
is valid. Reads work at unaligned offsets on either host byte order. The
`le` reads take the least significant byte first, the `be` reads the most
significant. A float read keeps the value's bits exactly, NaN payloads
included.
`read_name` validates the entire fixed-width field and returns the bytes
before its first NUL, or all `width` bytes if there is no NUL. It does not
validate padding or interpret the bytes as a particular text encoding.

title: Cursor and bounded subreaders
base64
text:
Base64 as RFC 4648 §4 defines it: the standard alphabet (`A`-`Z`, `a`-`z`,
`0`-`9`, `+`, `/`) and `=` padding. `import base64;` puts it in namespace
`base64`.

```goose
fn encode(out: u8[>..]&, src: const u8[:])            // appends 4 characters per 3 bytes, padded
fn decode(out: u8[>..]&, src: const u8[:]) -> bool    // appends the bytes; false if src is invalid
```

`decode` accepts only whole groups of four characters, the last of which
may end in `=` or `==`. It rejects line breaks, white space, unpadded text
and other alphabets (the `-` and `_` of the URL-safe alphabet are invalid).
It does not require the bits left over before the padding to be zero, so
`Zh==` decodes the same as `Zg==`; most decoders allow this. On invalid
input it returns `false` and leaves `out` as it was.

```goose
var text: u8[>..] = [];
base64::encode(text, "foobar");              // "Zm9vYmFy"
var bytes: u8[>..] = [];
if !base64::decode(bytes, text) { abort("not base64"); }
```

The codec computes the alphabet rather than looking it up, so the C
compiler vectorizes both loops. Both are also `simd fn`s (spec §7.12): when
clang builds for x86-64, they run as AVX2 or AVX-512 code on a CPU that
supports it, several times faster than with the baseline SSE2.

title: csv
text:
Comma-separated values as RFC 4180 defines them. `import csv;` puts the
reader and the writer's quoting in namespace `csv`.

```goose
fn each_record<F>(text: const u8[:], sep: u8 = ',') -> bool    // F(fields: const u8[:][:]) per record
fn format_field(out: u8[>..]&, s: u8[:], sep: u8 = ',')         // s, quoted where it needs to be
```

`each_record` passes each record's fields to its block, in order, as slices
of the text. Nothing is copied, and the slice of fields belongs to the
reader and is reused for the next record. A field may be quoted, and a
quoted field may contain separators, line breaks and doubled quotes, each
of which stands for one quote. A quoted field is passed without its
surrounding quotes, with its doubled quotes left as they are. Since a field
that is not quoted cannot contain a quote,
`format_replaced(out, field, "\"\"", "\"")` appends the text of any field.
Records end at LF or CRLF, except that the last record does not need to.
An empty line is a record of one empty field, and a header is a record like
any other. Spaces around a field are part of it. `sep` may be any byte
except a quote or a line break, such as `';'`, or `'\t'` for tab-separated
values.

`each_record` returns `false` at the first malformed record, after passing
every earlier record to its block; the block does not see the malformed
record. A record is malformed if it has a quote in a field that is not
quoted, a quoted field with no closing quote, or anything other than a
separator or a line break after a closing quote. A block's `return` leaves
the function that called `each_record`, as with every block.

```goose
var total = 0.0;
let ok = csv::each_record(text) { fields =>
    let price, valid = parse_flt(fields[2]);
    if valid { total += price; }
};
if !ok { abort("malformed CSV"); }
```

`format_field` appends `s` as it is or, if `s` contains the separator, a
quote or a line break, quoted with its quotes doubled. The caller writes the
separators between fields and the line break after a record.

```goose
for row in rows {
    csv::format_field(out, row.name);
    out.push(',');
    format(out, row.count, "\n");
}
```

title: json
text:
JSON as RFC 8259 defines it, three ways: a writer that appends values to a
builder, a parser that builds a document tree, and a reader that maps the
text directly onto the caller's own types, as a serde derive does.
`import json;` puts them in namespace `json`.

title: Writing
The document tree
text:
```goose
struct Node { next: Node&<u32>?, first: Node&<u32>?, key: const u8[:], val: Value }
enum Value { Null, Bool { v: bool }, Int { v: i64 }, Num { v: f64 }, Str { s: const u8[:] },
             Arr { count: i64 }, Obj { count: i64 } }
fn parse(text: u8[:], doc: Node[>..]&, decoded: u8[>..]&) -> Node?, u8[>..]
                                             // the root, or null and the error
fn member(n: Node?, key: u8[:]) -> Node?     // the first member named key; null if none
fn each<F>(n: Node&)                         // F(child) for each element or member, in order
fn as_f64(n: Node?) -> f64, bool             // an Int or a Num
fn as_i64(n: Node?) -> i64, bool             // an Int
fn as_bool(n: Node?) -> bool, bool
fn as_string(n: Node?) -> const u8[:], bool
```

`parse` pushes a node for every value onto `doc`, in text order. Each node
holds a link to its next sibling, a link to its first child (for a
container), its key (empty in an array) and its value. Keys and strings are
slices of `text`. Those that contained escapes are instead slices of their
decoded text, which is pushed onto `decoded`; nothing else is copied. A
number without a fraction or an exponent that fits an `i64` becomes an
`Int`. Any other number becomes a `Num`, correctly rounded, and infinite if
it is too large for an `f64`. Escapes decode to UTF-8: a surrogate pair
becomes one code point, and a lone surrogate becomes the three bytes that
encode its own code point. Strings are not checked to be valid UTF-8.

On
malformed text, `parse` returns null and a message naming the byte at which
it found the text malformed, such as
`json: expected ',' or '}' at byte 41`. The nodes before that point have
already been pushed.

The parser is a single loop
that keeps the open containers on a stack of its own, so nesting of any
depth can be parsed. `member` and the accessors accept a null node, so
lookups can be chained. Duplicate keys stay in the tree, and `member` finds
the first.

```goose
var doc: json::Node[>..] = [];
var decoded: u8[>..] = [];
let root, err = json::parse(text, doc, decoded);
guard root else { abort(err); }
let w, ok = json::as_i64(json::member(json::member(root, "window"), "width"));
let items = json::member(root, "items");
if items {
    json::each(items) { item =>
        let name, named = json::as_string(json::member(item, "name"));
        if named { print(name); }
    };
}
```

title: Reading into your own types
regex
text:
Regular expressions with the syntax and the matching rules of Rust's
`regex` crate, on bytes. `import regex;` puts them in namespace `regex`.

```goose
fn compile(pattern: u8[:]) -> Regex                  // aborts on a malformed pattern
fn compile(pattern: u8[:], err: u8[>..]&) -> Regex   // appends the error to err instead
fn find(re: Regex&, text: u8[:]) -> i64, i64         // the first match's start and end; -1, -1
fn matches(re: Regex&, text: u8[:]) -> bool          // whether there is a match
fn count(re: Regex&, text: u8[:]) -> i64             // the matches each_match finds
fn each_match<F>(re: Regex&, text: u8[:])            // F(start, end) for each match
fn each_captures<F>(re: Regex&, text: u8[:])         // F(caps: Captures) for each match
fn format_replaced<F>(out: u8[>..]&, re: Regex&, text: u8[:])
                                                     // text, each match replaced by F(caps)
struct Captures { text: const u8[:], slots: const i64[:] }
fn group(c: Captures, k: i64) -> const u8[:]         // group k's text; empty if it took no part
```

Matching is leftmost-first, as in the crate, Perl and most engines. The
match that starts earliest is chosen, and among the matches starting there,
the one the pattern prefers: alternatives are tried in order, and
repetitions are greedy unless they are lazy. Searches are unanchored. The
iterating functions find matches that do not overlap, from left to right,
and never find an empty match where the previous match ended: `a*` on
`baaa` matches at 0..0 and 1..4. Group 0 is the whole match, and the other
groups are numbered by their opening parentheses. Group k spans
`slots[2k]..slots[2k + 1]` of the text; both slots are -1 for a group that
took no part. A repeated group captures its last iteration. The slice that
`group` returns is rooted at the `Captures` the block was given. A view of
a group that has to outlive the block, such as a dictionary key, should
slice the text by the slots instead.

The supported syntax is:

* literal bytes;
* `.` (which matches a newline only under `s`);
* classes `[a-z]` and `[^...]`, where a `]` first or a `-` first or last is
  literal;
* `\d \w \s` and their complements `\D \W \S`, also inside classes;
* escapes `\n \t \r \f \v \xHH` and any punctuation (`\.`, `\\`);
* groups `(...)`, `(?:...)` and named groups `(?P<name>...)` or
  `(?<name>...)`, whose names are accepted but not used;
* flags `i` (letters match either case) and `s`, written `(?i)` to apply to
  the end of the group or `(?i:...)` to apply within, and `(?-i)` to turn
  one off;
* alternation `|`;
* `* + ? {n} {n,} {n,m}`, each made lazy by a `?` after it.

The classes and the case folding are ASCII, as the crate's are with Unicode
off. Anchors and word boundaries (`^ $ \A \z \b \B`), class set operations
(`&& -- ~~`), nested classes, Unicode classes and the other flags are not
supported, and `compile` reports them as errors:
`regex: anchors are not supported at offset 0 in ^a`. The module's header
describes two known differences from the crate: an alternation whose
branches share a repeating prefix is matched as written, as in Perl and
RE2, and groups at the end of a pattern under a `{0}` are kept.

`compile` builds complete DFAs up front: one that finds where a match ends,
and one over the reversed pattern that finds where it starts. A search
therefore takes one table lookup per byte of text it looks at. When every
match has rare leading bytes, or a rare byte after a part that cannot
contain that byte, the search skips through the text with `find_pair` or
`find_any` (above) and only looks where a match can be. Where the pattern
gives a group a fixed place in the match, the group is taken from that
place; otherwise it comes from a backtracker that runs over the match
alone. `find`, `matches` and `count` use neither.
A DFA can need exponentially many states, and a pattern whose program or
DFAs would grow too large (`[ab]*a[ab]{20}`, or counted repetitions in the
thousands) is reported as an error rather than compiled. Make the `Regex`
once, outside the loop that searches with it.

```goose
let re = regex::compile("(\\w+)=(\\d+)");
regex::each_captures(re, line) { c =>
    let n, ok = parse_int(regex::group(c, 2));
    if ok { settings.insert(line[c.slots[2]..c.slots[3]], n); }    // a key that outlives c
};

var err: u8[>..] = [];
let user = regex::compile(pattern_from_user, err);
if err.len > 0 { print(err); }

var out: u8[>..] = [];
let field = regex::compile("""\{\{\s*(\w+)\s*\}\}""");
regex::format_replaced(out, field, template) { caps =>
    let value = vars.get(regex::group(caps, 1));
    if value { value } else { "" }
};
```

title: gfx
text:
Graphics on SDL3's GPU API, which draws through Direct3D 12, Vulkan or Metal:
a window and its input, buffers, textures, samplers, pipelines, render and
compute passes, and reading results back. The module is optional: it needs a
compiler built with the `third_party/SDL` submodule, and a program using it
links what `goose --gfx-link msvc|cc` prints (a response file:
`cl game.c @<it>`, `cc game.c -o game @<it>`). A compiler built without it
still typechecks and generates C for such a program; only running the
program in-process fails. Everything is in namespace `gfx`;
`samples/27_gfx_cube.goose` is a small complete program, and the package's
[docs/gfx.md](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_gfx/blob/main/docs/gfx.md) says how it works.

**Text rendering is provided by [`ui`](#text-rendering-and-game-huds)**,
including fonts, positioned text and noninteractive game HUDs. Use
`ui::label` or `ui::draw_text`, then `ui::render` over the gfx scene. Only
specialized artwork or rendering requirements need a separate text renderer.

title: Shaders
text:
```goose
// Code shaders share, in a global each names as a part.
let scene = """
    layout(set = 1, binding = 0) uniform Scene { mat4 view_proj; };
    """;

// A shader's source after its stage, "vert", "frag" or "comp", or a file,
// .vert, .frag or .comp, relative to this one.
let vs = embed_shader("vert", scene, """
    layout(location = 0) in vec3 a_pos;
    void main() { gl_Position = view_proj * vec4(a_pos, 1.0); }
    """);
let fs = embed_shader("lit.frag");
```

`embed_shader` is a builtin. The GLSL 450 shader is compiled when the
program is, into SPIR-V, MSL and HLSL at once, and the result is a
`const u8[:]` of static data to pass to `pipeline` or `compute_pipeline`.
Its source is usually a `"""` string (spec §2) written at the call. It may
also come in several parts, each a string literal or a `let` or `const`
global initialized with one; the parts are joined as lines, in order. A
shader that does not compile is a compile error at the call. Where there is
an offending line of GLSL, the error points at it, in the program or in the
shader's file. `#include "x.glsl"` resolves relative to the shader's file,
or, for source written in the program, relative to the program's file. The
dialect is that of cute_spirv (`third_party/cute_spirv`): there are no
doubles and no geometry or tessellation stages, uniform blocks have no
instance names, and each storage buffer block holds one runtime array
(`buffer B { vec4 items[]; };`).

Resources go where SDL_GPU expects them, which the compiler checks:

| Stage | `set` | holds, each set's bindings numbered from 0 in this order |
|---|---|---|
| vertex | 0 | samplers, then storage textures, then storage buffers (read-only) |
| vertex | 1 | uniform blocks |
| fragment | 2 | samplers, then storage textures, then storage buffers (read-only) |
| fragment | 3 | uniform blocks |
| compute | 0 | samplers, then read-only storage textures, then read-only storage buffers |
| compute | 1 | read-write storage textures, then read-write storage buffers |
| compute | 2 | uniform blocks |

The `slot` of a `bind_*` call counts within one kind: the first storage buffer
is slot 0 no matter how many samplers precede it. A compute shader's
read-write resources are instead passed to `begin_compute` in binding order.

title: Device, window and frames
text:
```goose
fn open(title: const u8[:], width: i64, height: i64) -> bool        // and (..., flags)
fn open_headless(width: i64, height: i64) -> bool                   // no window; and (..., flags)
fn close()
fn frame() -> bool          // ends the frame drawn since the last call; false once asked to close
fn quit()                   // frame() returns false next
fn flush()                  // submit everything and wait for the GPU
fn error() -> u8[>..]       // why the last failing call failed
fn check()                  // abort if the program has misused gfx
fn driver() -> u8[>..]      // "direct3d12", "vulkan" or "metal"
fn set_title(title: const u8[:])
fn screen() -> Texture      fn screen_depth() -> Texture      fn screen_size() -> int2
fn time() -> f64            fn delta_time() -> f64            fn frame_count() -> i64
```

Flags for `open`: `WINDOW_RESIZABLE`, `WINDOW_HIDDEN`, `WINDOW_FULLSCREEN`,
`NO_VSYNC`, `DEBUG` (validation layers where installed; on in a debug build of
the layer). With `GOOSE_GFX_HEADLESS=1` in the environment, `open` opens no
window; the test runners use this. The screen is an RGBA8 texture the size
of the window in pixels, with a depth texture. A frame draws into it, and
`frame()` shows it. A window has the width and height that `open` gives, in
the display's own coordinates, and it has every pixel the display has in
that area. On a high-density display, that is more pixels than its width
and height; `screen_size()` counts these pixels, and the mouse position is
reported in them.

```goose
guard gfx::open("demo", 1280, 720) else { abort(str("gfx: ", gfx::error())); }
while gfx::frame() {
    gfx::begin_screen(float4 { 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 1.0 });
    // bind, uniforms, draw ...
    gfx::end_pass();
}
gfx::close();
```

Errors: a call that can fail for reasons outside the program returns false or
a zero handle, and `error()` says why. A call that the program should not
have made is printed when it happens and skipped, and the program aborts at
the next `frame()`, `check()`, read back or `close()`. Examples are a draw
with no pipeline bound, a texture the shader samples left unbound, a
released handle, and a uniform struct of the wrong size.

title: Input
text:
```goose
fn key_down(name: const u8[:]) -> bool        // SDL's key names: "A", "Space", "Left", "Escape"
fn key_pressed(name: const u8[:]) -> bool     // went down since the last frame()
fn key_released(name: const u8[:]) -> bool
fn mouse_down(button: i64) -> bool            // MOUSE_LEFT, MOUSE_MIDDLE, MOUSE_RIGHT
fn mouse_pressed(button: i64) -> bool         fn mouse_released(button: i64) -> bool
fn mouse_pos() -> float2    fn mouse_delta() -> float2      // in the screen's pixels
fn mouse_wheel() -> f32     fn mouse_in_window() -> bool    // over the window, or dragging from it
fn focused() -> bool                                      // keyboard focus at the last frame()
fn set_mouse_relative(on: bool) -> bool    fn mouse_relative() -> bool
fn set_cursor_visible(visible: bool) -> bool    fn cursor_visible() -> bool
fn inject_key(name: const u8[:], down: bool) -> bool           // as if typed, seen at the next frame()
fn inject_mouse(x: f32, y: f32, button: i64, down: bool)       // to pixel x, y; button 0 only moves
fn inject_text(text: const u8[:]) -> bool                      // an EVENT_TEXT per character
fn inject_focus(focused: bool) -> bool                        // simulate focus at the next frame()
fn events() -> Event[>..]           // the last frame's input, in the order it came
fn text_input(on: bool)             // typed text as EVENT_TEXT: off by default
fn scancode(name: const u8[:]) -> i64       fn key_name(scancode: i64) -> u8[>..]
fn clipboard() -> u8[>..]           fn set_clipboard(text: const u8[:]) -> bool
fn open_count() -> i64              // times gfx was opened: older handles are gone
```

The state functions report the state at a frame; `events()` reports what
happened between two frames, which text editing needs. The events are:

* key presses and releases, with their scancode, the character their key
  types (`keycode`) and the `MOD_*` keys held;
* typed characters;
* mouse motion;
* buttons (`MOUSE_*`, with X1 and X2), with their click count;
* the wheel.

When headless, gfx uses a clipboard of its own rather than the system's.

`mouse_pos` reports the mouse's position from the moment the window opens,
even before the mouse first moves. `mouse_in_window` is true while the
mouse is over the window, and while it holds a button that was pressed
there, as SDL reports it. For a window that opened under the mouse, SDL
reports this from the mouse's first move at the latest. Once the mouse
leaves, `mouse_pos` stays at the point where it left, off the screen, so
edge scrolling checks both. When headless, the mouse is in the window when
the last injected position is on the screen.

`set_mouse_relative(true)` confines the mouse to the window and hides its
cursor. `mouse_delta()` continues to report movement past the window edges,
in screen pixels: use it for first-person camera turns, rather than
`mouse_pos()`. Setting a different mode discards queued motion and clears
the current delta so a previously accumulated move cannot turn the camera.
Calling it again with the same mode preserves motion. It returns false on
failure, including a window without keyboard focus; `error()` gives the reason.

`set_cursor_visible(false)` hides the cursor for programs drawing their own.
Its preference applies outside relative mode: relative mode always hides the
cursor, and `cursor_visible()` reports that effective state inside the window.
The preference is restored when relative mode is disabled. Hiding a cursor
without focus fails; showing one always works while gfx is open.

`focused()` reports keyboard focus, which differs from `mouse_in_window()`.
`events()` includes `EVENT_FOCUS_GAINED` and `EVENT_FOCUS_LOST` in order with
other input; these kinds have no payload. Losing focus clears held keys and
buttons and mouse/wheel deltas, disables relative mode, and resets the cursor
to visible. Input received while unfocused is ignored. Focus gain leaves
relative mode disabled so a game can pause on focus loss and wait for a click
before recapturing. Held keys/buttons also get released edges and synthetic
up events before `EVENT_FOCUS_LOST`, so event-driven UI cannot retain a held
key or a drag across an application switch. `close()` also releases the
mouse and restores the cursor.

Headless gfx starts focused, with a visible cursor and relative mode disabled.
The setters simulate their state without touching the system mouse.
`inject_focus` queues the same transitions for testing; it does not change
operating-system focus. Closing and reopening resets all these states.

title: audio
text:
Procedural PCM sound effects over SDL3, independent of a window or graphics
device. `import audio;` uses the `audio::` namespace. It is a module of the
`gfx` package ([goose_gfx](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_gfx)). It is compiled into the
compiler with `-DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all` and otherwise built on first use;
`goose build` links it. See the package's [docs/audio.md](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_gfx/blob/main/docs/audio.md) for the mixer.

| Function | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `available() -> bool` | True when the native layer is linked; no device probe. |
| `open(sample_rate = 48000) -> bool` | Open the default output device, stereo output. |
| `open_offline(sample_rate = 48000) -> bool` | Open the same mixer without a device or background thread. |
| `close()` | Stop playback, free every sound, invalidate handles; safe to repeat. |
| `create_sound(samples: const f32[:], sample_rate = 48000, channels = 1) -> Sound` | Copy mono or interleaved stereo PCM into owned storage. |
| `release_sound(sound) -> bool` | Stop its voices and free the PCM. Zero is harmless. |
| `play(sound, volume = 1.0, pan = 0.0, pitch = 1.0, looping = false) -> Voice` | Start an independent voice, allowing overlapping repeats. |
| `playing(voice) -> bool` | Whether the voice is still mixing. Stale/zero handles return false. |
| `stop(voice)`, `stop_all()` | Stop one or every voice. Completed/stale/zero voices are harmless. |
| `set_voice(voice, volume, pan, pitch) -> bool` | Change a live voice without restarting. |
| `render(out: f32[:]) -> bool` | Offline only: write interleaved stereo output and advance playback. |
| `error() -> u8[>..]` | Most recent failure; successful calls do not clear it. |
| `error_into(out: u8[:]) -> i64` | Copy as much error text as fits, returning its full length. |

All calls run on the main thread; calls reachable from `thread_fn` are rejected.
`Sound { id: u64 }` and `Voice { id: u64 }` are explicit resources. Sound creation
copies the source immediately: Goose can then mutate or free its array. Releasing
a sound stops all its voices. Completed voices recycle automatically. A new
resource never aliases an old handle, even across `close()` and `open()`.

There is one mixer, at most `MAX_SOUNDS = 256` sounds and `MAX_VOICES = 64`
simultaneous voices. Exhaustion returns zero without stealing a voice. Rates
are 8000..192000 Hz. PCM must be nonempty, finite, in `[-1, 1]`, with complete
frames (two samples per stereo frame). Volume is `0..1`; pan is `-1..1`,
centered at zero, attenuating the opposite channel; pitch is `0.125..8` and
changes speed and duration together. Mixing uses linear interpolation and clips
the final sum to `[-1, 1]`. Leave headroom when many effects overlap.

Invalid arguments, stale sounds, unavailable devices and resource exhaustion
return false or a zero handle and set `error()`. They do not abort. Stopping or
querying a completed voice is normal; updating it returns false. Offline
`render` needs an even sample count, allows empty output, and advances exactly
`out.len / 2` frames. Device mode advances automatically; `playing()` describes
the mixer, so a little audio already buffered by the device can remain after
completion or stop. The module has no file decoding, streaming input,
recording, or effects.

```goose
import audio;
import math;
import os;

fn main() {
    if !audio::open() { print(audio::error()); return; }
    var pcm: f32[>..] = [];
    for i in 12000 {
        let t = i as f64 / 48000.0;
        let envelope = 1.0 - i as f64 / 12000.0;
        pcm.push((sin(TAU * 440.0 * t) * 0.2 * envelope) as f32);
    }
    let tone = audio::create_sound(pcm);
    let voice = audio::play(tone);
    while audio::playing(voice) { sleep_ms(5); }
    sleep_ms(100); // Let the device finish the already mixed tail.
    audio::close();
}
```

title: physics
text:
Rigid body physics on Box3D: worlds, bodies, shapes of every kind Box3D has,
nine kinds of joints, contact, sensor, hit, move and joint events, ray and
shape casts and overlap queries, a character mover, and recording and replay.
Like `gfx`, the module is optional: it needs a compiler built with the
`third_party/box3d` submodule, and a program using it links what
`goose --physics-link msvc|cc` prints (`cl game.c @<it>`,
`cc game.c -o game @<it>`; a program that also uses `gfx` adds gfx's
response file). A compiler built without it still typechecks and generates
C for such a program; only running the program in-process fails.
Everything is in namespace `physics`; `samples/28_physics_boxes.goose` is a
complete program, and the package's [docs/physics.md](https://github.com/aardappel/goose_physics/blob/main/docs/physics.md) says how it works.

The API is Box3D's under Goose names: `b3Body_GetPosition` is
`position(body)`, `b3CreateRevoluteJoint` is `create_revolute_joint`, a
getter uses the property name and a setter prefixes it with `set_`. Box3D
works in meters, kilograms and seconds and has no built-in up direction;
the default gravity is -10 along y. Where Box3D takes a callback, this API
uses other forms: events and query results come back as fresh arrays (each
also has an `_into` form that copies into a slice the caller provides and
returns how many there are), and friction and restitution mixing is chosen
from the `MIX_*` rules. Custom contact filters, pre-solve callbacks, debug
drawing and the standalone dynamic tree are not included.

Physics runs on the main thread; a `thread_fn` reaching it is a compile
error. Box3D spreads a step over worker threads of its own, as many as
`WorldDef.workers` asks for, and the results are the same for any number of
workers.

title: Errors
text:
A call that can fail for reasons outside the program, such as a file that
is not there or points that make no hull, returns false or a zero handle,
and `error()` says why. A call that the program should not have made is
reported when it happens and skipped, and the program aborts at the next
`step()`, `destroy(world)` or `check()`. Examples are a destroyed body, a
revolute function on a prismatic joint, and a height field on a dynamic
body. Every handle carries a generation, so using a destroyed object is
reported as an error instead of crashing.

```goose
fn error() -> u8[>..]           fn check()             fn misuse_count() -> i64
fn available() -> bool          fn version() -> Version          // Box3D's
fn byte_count() -> i64          // what Box3D has allocated
fn set_length_units_per_meter(units: f32)     // before anything else is made
fn length_units_per_meter() -> f32
fn world_count() -> i64         fn max_world_count() -> i64
```

shape's category is in the other's mask, unless they share a group index:
shapes in a positive group always collide, and shapes in a negative group
never do. A mesh collides only with
shapes that are not meshes. The default density is water's, 1000 kg/m³.

title: Geometry
text:
Hulls, meshes, height fields and baked compounds are made once and shared by
shapes. A shape keeps the geometry it was made from. Destroying a mesh,
height field or compound that shapes use releases the handle, and the data
is freed when the last shape using it is destroyed. A hull is copied into
each world that uses it.

The same geometry can also be queried on its own, in its own frame:
`compute_mass(g, density)` for spheres, capsules and hulls,
`compute_aabb(g, transform)`, `ray_cast(g, origin, translation,
