             →  < <= > >=  →  == != .== .!=  →  &&  →  ||
primary     := literal | qname | "null" | "self" | "(" expr ")"
             | arraylit | structlit | genericcall
genericcall := qname tyargs "(" args ")" trailingblock?
trailingblock := "{" (params "=>")? stmt* expr? "}"
sliceargs   := expr | bound? ".." bound?         // bound := "^"? expr
args        := (expr ("," expr)* ","?)?
arraylit    := "[" (exprlist ","? | expr ";" expr)? "]"
structlit   := (qname tyargs? | varianttype) "{" (fieldinits | fieldinits? "..")? "}"
fieldinits  := fieldinit ("," fieldinit)* ","?   // before "..": the "," required
fieldinit   := (ident ":")? expr
```

Known parse notes:

* The `structlit` vs `trailingblock` vs `blockexpr` ambiguity is resolved
  as in Rust (no struct literals or trailing blocks directly in
  `if`/`while`/`for`/`match`/`guard` scrutinee position).
* A statement that is a block-ended construct needs no `;` and ends at its
  `}` (§2).
* `f<` commits to a type argument list only when followed by `(`, `{`, or
  `.ident {` (§7.7); otherwise `<` is comparison.
* `T&<u8>` tokenizes as `&` `<` in type context only.
* `a..b` ranges exist only in `for` headers, slice brackets, and match arms.
* Multiple return types in a function *type* (not a declaration header)
  require parens around the list.
* `T&?` parses to the same type as `T?`, and `?` on an already-optional
  type is an error.
* `from` is not reserved: `return E from f` is recognized by the identifier
  that follows it, so `from` remains usable as a name.

---

title: Appendix E. Implementation notes (informative)
text:
What the current compiler does where the text above leaves it a choice. The
compiler's own description, pass by pass and analysis by analysis, is
`implementation.md`.

* **Two C backends.** The generated C is normally written to a file for a C
  compiler to build (`-o out.c`). Where the compiler was built with TinyCC
  (the `third_party/tinycc` submodule), giving no output file compiles that
  same C inside the compiler's own process instead and calls its `main`, so
  a program can run without a C toolchain and without writing a file. The
  program shares the compiler's process: its exit status becomes the
  compiler's, and the compiler's own progress lines go to stderr so that
  stdout is left to the program. It runs on the compiler's main thread. The
  compiler reserves that thread's stack at 64 MB on Windows and macOS,
  where an executable's main thread gets 1 MB and 8 MB respectively by
  default; on Linux it is the stack limit the process started with
  (`ulimit -s`), as for an executable. The program's own C is the same for
  both backends, and `-D` is written into that C rather than passed to a
  backend so that this stays true. What differs is the runtime around it.
  The in-process build compiles the whole runtime with the program. The
  file holds only the parts of the runtime that have to be inlined into the
  program and declares the rest; `goose --emit-runtime` writes that rest as
  a C file of its own, built once and linked with every program
  (`--standalone` writes a file that holds the whole runtime, as the
  in-process build does). TinyCC does not optimize and cannot place
  thread-local storage in an in-memory run, so a program that uses workers
  (§11.2) is refused there (docs/design/jit_backend.md).
* **Fat references.** A callee that grows a resizable through a reference
  (`push` through a `f64[>..]&`) must know which data stack to bump. The
  compiler does not pin that stack per call site (§10.2): every reference
  to a resizable-class value carries the stack identity beside the header
  address (C.2), and a pool reference (§5.4) carries the freelist as well.
  There is no surface syntax; the form is per instantiation, and a variable
  keeps the one its first binding gives it (§5.4).
* **Stack assignment** uses the hidden-argument strategy permitted by §10.3.
  Every function that uses data stacks receives a base index as a hidden
  argument and addresses its nonfixed locals at constant offsets from that
  base. Callees start above the function's in-use watermark. All stacks
  reachable by the program are reserved when its thread program starts; their
  count is known at compile time (§7.8).
  The globals of a program instance, together with the dedicated stacks of
  the resizable globals, form one struct reached through a single
  thread-local pointer (a plain pointer in a program without workers).
  Main's struct is a static instance; a worker's is allocated when the
  worker starts and filled from the spawn image, which carries the used
  globals after the arguments. The only C statics are string literals and
  `const` globals with compile-time initializers. Every generated function
  is shared between thread programs and the main program.
* **Element-run results** (§7.3) exist for variable *array* results
  (`T[]`): an element-run receiver compiles the callee a second time in run
  form (raw elements plus a count out-parameter), so `v.append(f())` is
  contiguous with no copy, and a named result incurs the specified single
  callee-side copy. Callees with no run form (builtins, tag dispatch) fall
  back to the value form, and the receiver slides the length prefix out
  with one memmove. A runtime-capacity limited result is built on the
  destination stack, then compacted there to discard its header and unused
  slots. Non-array variable results have only the value form.
* **Queue images** (§11.2) are one contiguous byte image per value; a
  resizable's is its count, its fixed fields and its tail's elements, built
  on a scratch stack at `qput` and unpacked at the receiver's destination.
* **C locals at function scope.** Every aggregate-typed C local (a struct,
  array, slice or header) is declared at the top of its C function rather
  than in the block that uses it, and a literal temporary with unused
  limited-array slots is zero-initialized. Both work around MSVC
  19.44–19.51. At any optimization level it miscompiles a read through a
  copy of a struct that holds the address of a block-scoped local (for
  example a slice of a fixed array declared in a loop body, passed to an
  inlined callee), and it exploits the indeterminate bytes of a copied,
  partially written struct. Neither workaround changes what the program
  means.
* **The store record.** Every store of a reference, slice, or value holding
  one, into a variable, field, element or global, is logged program-wide
  with the stored value's root, exactness, and source container. A
  specialization also summarizes the stores into its parameters' pointees,
  and these summaries are replayed onto the caller's containers at each
  call. A grow-only shrink (§5.1) checks this record for any live value
  that holds a reference into the array, following source links (a copy
  holds what its source holds; a global source is checked by its type). A
  shrink inside a loop is checked again at the loop's end against the
  stores that the rest of the body made.
* **Liveness at a shrink.** The checker keeps the statement index of every
  open block; a holder is live when its name occurs in a later statement
  of an open block at or inside its scope, in that block's tail, or
  anywhere in an enclosing loop it outlives. Nested functions in scope are
  followed by name from the calls in that code. What a `for` walks in
  place, and the references and slices on the path to it that the loop
  loads again, are live throughout its body (§6.5).
* **Literal parameters** (§7.7). Which parameters are literals is part of
  the specialization key; their values are not. A read of a literal
  parameter is a value that is not constant-folded but keeps the literal's
  adaptability. Every adaptation of the bare parameter is recorded on the
  specialization with its line, and a literal parameter passed on as a
  literal records a link to the callee's parameter. After the whole program
  is checked, each call site's literal is verified against the closure of
  those records. The parameter is passed at its nominal type (`int64_t`,
  `double`), and each use casts it to the type it adapted to; the
  verification proved that cast exact.

title: The goose command line
text:
One executable, `goose`, is the compiler, the in-process runner, the build
tool, the package fetcher, the formatter and the language server. This page
describes all of it. `goose help` prints a summary, and `goose help
<command>` the options of one command. How a program uses libraries, and how
to make one, is in [packages.md](packages.md).

title: 1. Commands
text:
```
goose <command> file.goose [options] [-- program args...]
goose file.goose [options] [-- program args...]
```

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `goose run file.goose` | Compile the program and run it in this process ([§2](#2-running-a-program)). `goose file.goose` is the same. |
| `goose build file.goose` | Build an executable with a C compiler on this machine ([§3](#3-building-an-executable)). |
| `goose check file.goose` | Parse and typecheck the program, and write and run nothing ([§4](#4-checking-a-program)). |
| `goose fetch file.goose` | Fetch the packages the program declares ([§7](#7-packages)). |
| `goose format file.goose\|dir...` | Rewrite files in the standard layout ([§9](#9-formatting)). |
| `goose toolchain` | Report the C compiler, cmake and git found, and `GOOSE_HOME` ([§11](#11-toolchain-version-help-and-completion)). |
| `goose version` | Print the compiler's version and its runtime's. |
| `goose lsp` | Serve an editor over the Language Server Protocol ([§10](#10-the-language-server)). |
| `goose completion <shell>` | Print a completion script for bash, zsh, fish or PowerShell. |
| `goose help [command]` | Print the help, on everything or on one command. |

The command comes first. A first argument that is not a command is read as
an option or a file, so `goose file.goose` runs the program. A first word
with no dot or slash in it, which is neither a command nor an existing
file, is taken as a mistyped command: `goose biuld x.goose` suggests
`build` and does nothing.

Options may come before or after the file, in any order. Each command takes
one program, its *root file*: the file that holds `main` and declares the
program's packages. Everything after `--` belongs to the program being run.
`--help` or `-h` anywhere before a `--` prints the help on the command given,
and `goose --version` is `goose version`.

title: 2. Running a program
text:
```bash
goose hello.goose
goose run hello.goose -- input.txt --verbose
```

`goose run` compiles the program to C, compiles that C in memory with the
TinyCC compiler built into `goose`, and runs it in the compiler's own
process. There is no build step and no file is written. On Windows nothing
else is needed. On Linux the C library's headers are needed (`libc6-dev` or
`glibc-devel`), and on macOS the SDK of the Xcode command line tools.

The arguments after `--` are the program's. The `os` module gives them to
the program, with argument 0 being the root file's path as it was given:

<!-- check-only -->
```goose
import os;

fn main() {
    let a = args();                      // a[0] is the program
    guard a.len > 1 else { print("usage: hello file..."); exit(2); }
    for i in 1..a.len { print(i, ": ", a[i]); }
}
```

`goose run` exits with the program's exit code: 0 when `main` returns,
the code given to `exit(code)`, and 1 when the program fails a check or
calls `abort` (`goose runtime error: ...` on stderr). A program that does
not compile also exits with 1, after its errors.

What a run cannot do, a build can:

* A program that starts threads must be built. TinyCC cannot place the
  thread-local storage that each worker's data stacks are kept in, so
  `goose run` refuses it.
* TinyCC does not optimize, so a run is for trying things out, and
  timing is done on a build.
* A run keeps its data relative to the root file: `resource_dir()`
  returns the root file's directory, where a built program's is the
  executable's ([stdlib.md](stdlib.md#os)). Relative paths are relative to
  the working directory either way.

A program whose packages have C of their own still runs this way. Packages
compiled into `goose` (`goose toolchain` lists them) need nothing more. The
C of any other package, and the program's own C named in its sidecar
([packages.md](packages.md#3-a-program-with-c-of-its-own)), is built into
a shared library with a C compiler on the machine, once, and loaded into
the run. `--cc` picks that compiler as it does for a build, and `-v` prints
the commands that build it.

`goose run` takes the options in [§5](#5-options-for-run-build-and-check).
It takes no `-o`: the flag form `goose -o out.c` writes C instead
([§8](#8-writing-the-c-yourself)).

title: 3. Building an executable
text:
```bash
goose build hello.goose && ./hello
goose build -o out/hello hello.goose     # the executable elsewhere
goose build --debug hello.goose          # checked, with debug information
goose build --dry-run hello.goose        # print the commands and run none
```

`goose build` writes the program's C, compiles it with a C compiler on the
machine, and links it with the runtime and the native parts of the packages
the program uses. The executable goes beside the root file, named after it
(`hello`, or `hello.exe` on Windows), unless `-o` or the sidecar's
`output = "name";` names it. The build prints `built <executable>` when it
is done.

The C compiler is the first of these that names one:

1. `--cc name|path`
2. the `GOOSE_CC` environment variable
3. `cc = "clang";` in `GOOSE_HOME/config` (`~/.goose/config`)
4. the first compiler found on the machine.

A name is one of `msvc` (or `cl`), `clang-cl`, `clang`, `gcc` and `cc`, and
a path names the compiler's executable. Without a request, Windows looks for
`cl` on `PATH` (as in a Developer Command Prompt), then `clang-cl` and
`clang` in Visual Studio's LLVM or on `PATH`, then MSVC through Visual
Studio's `vcvars64.bat`, then `gcc` and `cc` on `PATH`. Other systems look
for `cc`, `gcc` and `clang` on `PATH`. `goose toolchain` shows which one a
build would use, and why. Setting up Visual Studio's environment takes a
second or two, so `goose` keeps the result in `GOOSE_HOME/toolchain` and
`goose toolchain --refresh` sets it up again.

The C is always compiled optimized (`/O2` or `-O2`), whatever `-O` level
the Goose compiler used, except under `--debug`. The options of a build,
beyond those in [§5](#5-options-for-run-build-and-check):

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `-o exe` | Where the executable goes. Its directory is made if needed. |
| `--debug` | Turn on the overflow, range and tag checks (`GS_DEBUG=1`), and build the C without optimization and with debug information (`/Od /Zi`, or `-O0 -g`), for a debugger. |
| `--cc name\|path` | The C compiler, as above. |
| `--standalone` | Compile the runtime into the program, rather than linking the runtime object built once per C compiler. |
| `-v` | Print each command the build runs, and what it prints. |
| `--dry-run` | Print the commands the build would run, with their paths, and run none of them. A Makefile or CMake project can take them from here. |

Everything a build makes along the way goes under `GOOSE_HOME`. The program's
C, objects and logs go in `build/prog/<name>-<hash>/`, one directory per
root file. The runtime object is compiled the first time a C compiler is
used, once per compiler and per release or debug configuration, into
`build/runtime/`. When a compile or link fails, the error shows the command
and what it printed, and says where the log is.

title: 4. Checking a program
text:
```bash
goose check hello.goose
```

`goose check` parses and typechecks the program and everything it imports,
including the lifetime and bounds checks the compiler makes, and writes and
runs nothing. It prints nothing when the program is correct, and its errors
and exit code 1 when it is not. It takes the options in
[§5](#5-options-for-run-build-and-check). `--diagnostics json` gives an
editor or another tool the errors as data ([§6](#6-what-goose-prints)), and
with `--stacks` a check also reports the program's data stacks.

title: 5. Options for run, build and check
text:
These options have the same meaning for `goose run`, `goose build`,
`goose check` and the flag form `goose -o out.c`.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `-O0`, `-O1`, `-O2` | How much the Goose compiler inlines: nothing, a little, or the most (the default). Constant folding and propagation run at every level, and a build's C compiler optimizes at every level. |
| `--debug` | Turn on the overflow checks, the range checks of `as` casts and the tag checks (`GS_DEBUG=1`). Each failure names its source line, and an overflow or a cast names the values involved. A build also gets debug information ([§3](#3-building-an-executable)). |
| `-D NAME[=VALUE]` | Define a C macro in the generated program, as `-DNAME[=VALUE]` does too. The define is written into the C itself, so a run and a build see the same source. The value is 1 when none is given. |
| `--stack-reserve size` | The address space reserved for each data stack, from 64K up to 256T with a `K`, `M`, `G` or `T` suffix. The default is 2G. The address space is committed as it is used, so a large reservation costs nothing until it is used. |
| `--stacks` | Report how many data stacks the program and each of its workers use, what that adds up to, and the cap it puts on `hardware_threads()`. |
| `--bce-lines` | Report, for each source line, how many bounds checks the compiler removed and how many it kept. |
| `--no-bce` | Keep every bounds check. `checkfree` functions are then not verified, and the compiler warns about that. |
| `--specs` | Print every specialization of each function, after optimization, as source. |
| `--stats` | Print a few lines about what the compile did: the declarations parsed, the specializations and optimizations, the bounds checks removed, and the files written. |
| `--color auto\|always\|never` | Whether errors and warnings are in color ([§6](#6-what-goose-prints)). |
| `--diagnostics text\|json` | Print errors and warnings as text on stderr (the default), or as JSON on stdout ([§6](#6-what-goose-prints)). |
| `--offline` | Fetch nothing: a package that is not fetched yet is an error at its import ([§7](#7-packages)). |
| `--update` | Fetch the packages declared at a tag or branch again ([§7](#7-packages)). |
| `--stdlib dir` | Where the standard library is ([§12](#12-environment-and-files)). |
| `--cc name\|path` | The C compiler for anything that needs one ([§3](#3-building-an-executable)). |
| `-v` | Print each command that builds C, and what it prints. |

The `-D` macros that the runtime reads, which configure a program:

| Macro | Default | What it sets |
|---|---|---|
| `GS_DEBUG` | 0 | 1 is what `--debug` sets: the overflow, range and tag checks. |
| `GS_STACK_STATS` | 0 | 1 makes each thread program report its data stack use on stderr as it ends. |
| `GS_STACK_RESERVE` | 2 GB | The address space reserved per data stack, which `--stack-reserve` sets. |
| `GS_STACK_GAP` | 1 MB | The unmapped gap after each data stack, which makes runaway growth abort. |
| `GS_STACK_BUDGET` | 32 TB | The address space all thread programs together are meant to take; `hardware_threads()` is capped at what it has room for. |
| `GS_MAX_STACKS` | 1024 | The most data stacks one thread program may use. A program that needs more fails to compile. |
| `GS_SIMD` | 2 | The highest CPU level for `simd` functions' versions under clang on x86-64: 0 or 1 lowers it. |

A program that runs out of a data stack ends with a message that names
`--stack-reserve`. `--stacks` and `-DGS_STACK_STATS=1` show how many stacks
a program uses, and the [implementation
notes](implementation.md#7-the-runtime) explain how they are reserved.

title: 6. What goose prints
text:
A run prints only what the program prints. A check that succeeds prints
nothing, and a build prints only the `built` line. Errors and warnings go to
stderr, each with the line of source it is about. `--stats` adds a few lines
about the compile, on stdout, or on stderr for a run, whose stdout is the
program's.

Errors and warnings are in color on a terminal. `--color never`, or a
non-empty `NO_COLOR`, turns color off. `--color always`, or a
`CLICOLOR_FORCE` other than 0, turns it on wherever the output goes.

Work that takes a while, such as fetching a package, building a package's C
or compiling the runtime, prints one line on stderr as it starts. On a
terminal, a live line below it shows what is running, for how long, and the
last line the tool printed, and it is erased when the work is done. When
stderr goes anywhere else (a file, a pipe, a CI log, an agent running the
command), or `TERM` is `dumb`, there is no live line, only the one-line
notes. `GOOSE_PROGRESS=plain` or `GOOSE_PROGRESS=live` overrides that
choice, and `-v` and `--dry-run` always use plain output.

`--diagnostics json` prints the errors and warnings on stdout as a JSON
array, after anything a run's program printed. What `goose` itself would
have printed on stdout, the `--stats` lines and a build's `built` line,
goes to stderr instead. The exit code stays what it would be:

```json
[
  {"severity": "error", "message": "expected a value of type i32, got const u8[:]",
   "file": "bad.goose", "line": 1, "col": 26, "endLine": 1, "endCol": 29,
   "related": [{"message": "in fn main() instantiated from bad.goose:1",
                "file": "bad.goose", "line": 1, "col": 1}],
   "text": "bad.goose:1: error: expected a value of type i32, got const u8[:]\n..."}
]
```

Each object has a `severity` (`error` or `warning`) and a `message`. Where
the place is known, it also has the `file` as the compiler names it, a
1-based `line` and byte `col`, and `endLine` and `endCol` one past the last
byte. `related` holds the lines that follow the message, in the same form,
and `text` holds the whole message as the terminal would have shown it.
An error that is not about the program, such as a missing C compiler, has a
message and text only.

title: 7. Packages
text:
A program that imports a package that has not been fetched yet fetches it
with git into `GOOSE_HOME/pkg` the first time it is run, built or checked,
and builds the package's C there once per C compiler.
[packages.md](packages.md) describes how a program declares its packages.

```bash
goose fetch app.goose               # fetch what app.goose declares, and compile nothing
goose fetch --update app.goose      # fetch packages at a tag or a branch again
goose run --offline app.goose       # fetch nothing; a package not fetched is an error
```

`goose fetch` makes a later session work without a network. A package
pinned to a commit is never fetched again. One pinned to a tag or a branch
is fetched again only with `--update`, which every command that compiles
also takes. The language server never fetches anything.

When a tool that is needed is missing, the error names it: git to fetch,
cmake for a package built with CMake, and a C compiler for any C code. A
program that has no C of its own and uses no package with C needs none of
them. Deleting `GOOSE_HOME` loses nothing that a build cannot recreate
([packages.md](packages.md#5-the-cache) shows what is in it).

title: 8. Writing the C yourself
text:
`goose build` covers most needs, and `goose build --dry-run` shows the
commands it runs. To build the C in a build system of your own, or to link
a Goose program into a C or C++ host, give the compiler an output file
instead of a command:

```bash
goose -o tour.c tour.goose                    # the program's C
goose --emit-runtime goose_runtime.c          # the runtime's C
cc -O2 -c goose_runtime.c                     # once, with the programs' compiler and flags
cc -O2 tour.c goose_runtime.o -o tour -lm -pthread
```

On Windows the last two are `cl /O2 /c goose_runtime.c` and
`cl /O2 tour.c goose_runtime.obj`. On Linux, add `-ldl` before glibc 2.34.

`-o out.c` writes the program's C and runs nothing; `--jit` also runs the
program in-process as `goose run` would. The C holds the program and the part
of the runtime that is inlined into it. The rest of the runtime (the OS
layer, the reservation of data stacks, threads and printing) is the C that
`--emit-runtime` writes, which is compiled once and linked with every
program. It takes no `-D` of its own, since a program hands the runtime its
configuration as it starts. Build it with the same C compiler and flags as
the programs. A program from another version of the compiler fails to link
against it (`goose version` prints the runtime's hash, which must match).

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `-o out.c` | Write the program's C, and do not run it. |
| `--standalone` | Write C that holds the whole runtime, and builds on its own: `cc -O2 tour.c -o tour -lm -pthread`. |
| `--header out.h` | Also write a header for a C host, declaring the program's `export fn`s, of which there must be one at least. The C then has no `main`: the host calls `goose_init(argc, argv)` once, which runs the program's `main`, and then calls the exported functions. |
| `--include header.h` | Have the generated C include this header, for small shims written against the generated types (spec §7.10). May be repeated. |
| `--jit` | Also run the program in this process. |
| `--emit-runtime out.c` | Write the runtime's C. |
| `--<package>-link msvc\|cc` | Print the path of the response file that links the native part of a package compiled into `goose`, for the `msvc` or `cc` style of command line. |

The [tutorial](tutorial.md#19-calling-goose-from-c) and the
[reference](reference.md#export-fn) show a C host. All the options in
[§5](#5-options-for-run-build-and-check) apply too, `-O` and `-D` among
them.

A program that uses `audio`, `gfx`, `physics` or `ui` also links that
package's native part. When the package is compiled into `goose`, its
response file is part of the compiler's installation:

```bash
cc -O2 cube.c goose_runtime.o -o cube @$(goose --gfx-link cc) -lm -pthread
```

A `ui` program puts the `ui` response file before the `gfx` one it draws
through. For packages that are not compiled in, and for a program's own C,
`goose build --dry-run` prints the commands that build each native part and
the response file it makes.

title: 9. Formatting
text:
```bash
goose format src/                  # rewrite every .goose file under src/
goose format --check .             # list the files that are not formatted
goose format < in.goose > out.goose
```

`goose format` rewrites each file in place in the standard layout: the
indentation, the spaces between tokens, blank lines and trailing commas.
Line breaks stay where they are. A directory stands for the `.goose` files
under it, except those in directories whose names start with a dot and in
build trees (directories holding a `CMakeCache.txt`). With no file, or `-`,
it formats standard input to standard output. A file that does not parse is
left as it is, and its errors are printed.

`--check` writes nothing and lists the files that are not formatted. The
exit status is 0 when every file is formatted (or now is), 1 when `--check`
found one that is not, and 2 when a file does not parse or cannot be read or
written, or an option is wrong. [editors.md](editors.md#formatting) shows how
to format on save.

title: 10. The language server
text:
```bash
goose lsp
```

`goose lsp` serves an editor over the Language Server Protocol on stdin
and stdout: diagnostics as files change, hover, go to definition,
references and rename, symbols, semantic highlighting, signature help,
completion, inlay hints, folding, code lenses and formatting. It analyzes
the programs whose root files the editor names in its
`initializationOptions` (`entryFiles`), and every open file that none of
them imports. It never fetches a package: one that is not fetched yet is an
error at its import, which `goose fetch` resolves.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--stdio` | Serve on stdin and stdout, as it does anyway. Clients pass it. |
| `--stdlib dir` | Where the standard library is. |
| `--probe` | Print the protocol version (`goose lsp 3.17`) and exit. |

The [VS Code extension](../vscode/README.md) starts the server itself;
[editors.md](editors.md) has the configuration for Neovim, Helix and
Emacs, and the [design notes](design/language_server.md) the details.

title: 11. toolchain, version, help and completion
text:
`goose toolchain` reports the C compiler a build would use (its name,
version, path, the style of its command line and how it was found), its C++
driver, cmake, git, the packages compiled into `goose`, and `GOOSE_HOME`.
It exits with 1 when there is no C compiler. It takes `--cc` to look for a
particular compiler, `--json` for a report as JSON, and `--refresh` to set
up Visual Studio's environment again rather than take the one kept from
last time.

`goose version`, or `goose --version`, prints the compiler's version and
its runtime's: a hash of the runtime's text, which the runtime that
`--emit-runtime` writes must match.

`goose help` lists the commands and the common options; `goose help
<command>` (or `goose <command> --help`) the options of one. `goose help c`
covers writing the C yourself, and `goose help internals` the options in
[§14](#14-options-for-working-on-the-compiler). `goose help --man` prints
all of it as a man page, which a release ships as `man/goose.1`.

`goose completion bash` (or `zsh`, `fish`, `powershell`) prints a script
that completes the commands, their options and `.goose` files. To have it in
every shell:

```bash
goose completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/goose
goose completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_goose"
goose completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/goose.fish
goose completion powershell >> $PROFILE
```

or, for the shell at hand, `source <(goose completion bash)`.

title: 12. Environment and files
text:
| Variable | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GOOSE_HOME` | Where fetched packages, build intermediates and settings go. The default is `~/.goose` (`%USERPROFILE%\.goose` on Windows). |
| `GOOSE_CC` | The C compiler, where `--cc` is not given. |
| `GOOSE_STDLIB` | The standard library's directory, where `--stdlib` is not given. |
| `GOOSE_PROGRESS` | `plain` or `live`: how progress shows on stderr. |
| `NO_COLOR` | Set and not empty: no color, unless `--color` says otherwise. |
| `CLICOLOR_FORCE` | Set to anything but 0: color, even when stderr is not a terminal. |
| `GOOSE_TCCLIB` | Where TinyCC's headers and support library are, for a compiler moved away from both its installation and its build tree. |

Without `--stdlib` or `GOOSE_STDLIB`, the compiler looks for the standard
library in a `stdlib` directory beside its executable, then in the parent
directories up to three levels above it, which finds a release's and a
source tree's, and last in `./stdlib`.

`GOOSE_HOME/config` holds settings that apply to every build. It is written
like a sidecar, and its one setting is the C compiler:

<!-- fragment -->
```goose
// ~/.goose/config
cc = "clang";
```

A program's *sidecar*, `foo.build` beside `foo.goose`, names the program's
own C, the libraries it links and the executable's name
([packages.md](packages.md#3-a-program-with-c-of-its-own)). The cache under
`GOOSE_HOME` is described in [packages.md](packages.md#5-the-cache).

title: 13. Exit status
text:
| Command | Exit status |
|---|---|
| `run` | The program's: 0 when `main` returns, the code it passes to `exit`, and 1 when it aborts. 1 when it does not compile. |
| `build`, `check`, `fetch`, `-o` | 0 on success, 1 on an error in the program, a failed C compile or a failed fetch. |
| `format` | 0 when every file is formatted, 1 when `--check` found one that is not, 2 on a file that does not parse or a wrong option. |
| `toolchain` | 1 when there is no C compiler. |
| any | 1 on a wrong option, a mistyped command, or a missing file. |

title: 14. Options for working on the compiler
text:
These look into what the compiler does, and serve its test suite
([testing.md](testing.md)). `goose help internals` lists them.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--tokens` | Print the file's tokens. |
| `--parse` | Stop after parsing. |
| `--check` | Stop after typechecking, as `goose check` does. |
| `--dump` | Print the parsed program back as source. |
| `--dump-docs` | Print the documentation comments of the program's declarations, fields and variants. |
| `--dump-file out` | Write that dump to a file, and go on. |
| `--roundtrip` | Check that the dump parses and dumps back to itself. |
| `--multi-test file...` | Compile each file as a run of its own would, and end what each printed with a line on stdout and stderr: `==== goose --multi-test: exit <code> <file>`. A `%` in `-o` stands for each file's name. |
| `--bce-test` | Verify the `// bce:elide` and `// bce:keep` annotations in the source. |
| `--unsafe-no-rf-check` | Leave out the checks after calls that a `return ... from` can pass through. This is unsound, and is only for measuring what they cost. |
| `--gen-runtime-header` | Regenerate `src/runtime_inline.h` from `src/runtime/` (`GOOSE_RUNTIME` names that directory if it is not found). |
| `--compile-shader file` | Print what a shader compiles to, without a program around it; `--shader-source msl` or `hlsl` prints that source as well. |

`goose format --verify file.goose|dir...` formats each file in memory and
writes nothing. It checks the result as a format does, and that formatting
it again changes nothing, and it skips a file that does not parse. Setting
`GOOSE_ROUNDS` in the environment makes the typechecker trace what keeps a
recursive cycle's rounds going.

title: Building programs and using packages
text:
This page explains how to turn a Goose program into an executable, how to
use libraries that are not part of the compiler, and how to make such a
library. The design behind this, and how the compiler implements it, are
described in [design/packages.md](design/packages.md).

title: 1. Running and building
text:
`goose foo.goose` (or `goose run foo.goose`) compiles the program into the
compiler's own process and runs it there, with no C compiler and no build
step. `goose build foo.goose` makes an executable, `foo` or `foo.exe`,
beside the source, with a C compiler found on the machine:

```bash
goose build foo.goose && ./foo
goose build --dry-run foo.goose         # print the commands instead of running them
```

`goose toolchain` shows which C compiler a build uses, and `--cc clang`,
`GOOSE_CC` or `cc = "clang";` in `~/.goose/config` selects another. The
runtime and the C of each package are compiled once per C compiler, and an
executable is linked with the native parts of the packages it uses. A run
builds the same native parts into a library that it loads, unless the
package is compiled into the compiler. Everything the compiler produces
along the way goes under `~/.goose` (`GOOSE_HOME` moves it,
[§5](#5-the-cache)).

[The command line](command_line.md) describes the rest: every option of
run, build and check, what the compiler prints, and how to write the C
for a build system of your own.

title: 2. Using a package
text:
A *package* is a library in a directory of its own: a module named after it,
`name.goose`, further modules beside it, and possibly C. The packages the
compiler knows by name are the *blessed* ones (`src/blessed.txt`). A program
imports them like any other module:

```goose
import gfx;
import physics;
```

The first time, the compiler fetches the package from its repository at the
pinned tag into `~/.goose/pkg`, builds its C with cmake and the C compiler,
and keeps both. A compiler configured with
`-DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all` has the blessed packages compiled in and runs
such a program with nothing else installed; `goose toolchain` lists what is
built in.

Any other package, or another version of a blessed one, is declared in the
program's *root file* (the one named on the command line), with its source:

```goose
import mylib from "joe/mylib@v2";                  // GitHub, at tag v2
import mylib from "github.com/joe/mylib@3f2c1a9";  // any host, at a commit
import mylib from "https://git.example.com/x/mylib.git@main";   // any git URL, at a branch
import mylib from "../mylib";                      // a directory, used in place
```

`import name from "source";` declares the package `name` and imports its
module `name.goose`; its other modules are imported with
`import name.other;`. A git source needs a ref after `@`. A tag or a commit
pins the package. A branch does too, until
`goose fetch --update program.goose` fetches it again. A path is relative
to the file that contains the import, and nothing is copied: you can edit
the library and run the program.

**Only the root file declares packages.** Every other file, including the
library's own files, imports by name alone. A library that needs another package
writes the same `import other from "…";` line in its own files, and the
compiler reads it as a *requirement*: if the root does not declare `other`,
the error says exactly what line to add to the root. If the root declares
the same package from a different ref, the compiler warns; if it declares
it from a different source, that is an error. So a program's dependencies
are flat, pinned and in one place, and a program contains only one version
of each package.

`goose fetch program.goose` fetches everything the root declares, for a
later offline session, and `--offline` makes any command fetch nothing.
When a tool that is needed is missing, the error
names it: `git` to fetch, `cmake` for a package built with CMake, and a C
compiler for any C code. A program with no C and no such packages needs
none of them.

title: 3. A program with C of its own
text:
C that belongs to the program goes in a sidecar beside the root file,
`foo.build` beside `foo.goose`:

```goose
// foo.build
c_sources = ["impl.c", "vendor/stb_impl.c"];   // compiled with the program's build
c_include = ["vendor"];
c_defines = ["IMPL_FAST=1"];
c_flags_cc = ["-mavx2"];                       // compile flags for gcc and clang; c_flags_msvc for MSVC
c_libs = ["m"];                                // system libraries, by name
c_libs_windows = ["user32"];                   // one platform's part
dylibs_linux = ["SDL2=libSDL2-2.0.so.0"];      // what an extern "SDL2" block opens here
output = "foo";                                // the executable's name, if not the file's
```

The file looks like Goose (`//` comments, `key = value;`, strings, `true`
and `false`, `[lists]`), and every `c_*` key can take a `_windows`,
`_linux` or `_macos` suffix for a part that applies to one platform only.
`goose build` compiles and links that C; `goose run` builds it into a
library that the in-process run loads. Either way, an `extern fn` in the
program can call it:

```goose
extern fn impl_sum(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32;
extern fn impl_count(s: const u8[:], c: u8) -> i64;   // a slice arrives as { data, len }
```

A single-header library needs only one `impl.c` that defines its
implementation macro and includes the header. Alternatively,
`--include shim.h` on the command line splices a header into the generated
C; this still works for small shims written against the generated types
(spec §7.10, [command_line.md](command_line.md#8-writing-the-c-yourself)).

title: 4. Making a package
text:
A package is a git repository (or any directory) laid out like this:

```
mylib/
  mylib.goose        the entry: `namespace mylib;`, its declarations
  mylib.build        the sidecar, when there is C to build (optional)
  extra.goose        another module: `import mylib.extra;`
  src/, include/     the C, if any
  examples/, test/   programs of its own, each a root file
  README.md
```

Inside the package, `import helper;` finds `helper.goose` under the
package's root, `import .helper;` finds it relative to the importing file,
and `import std;` reaches the standard library. By convention a package's
files declare its name as their namespace.

A library that needs another package writes the requirement in its entry
file, `import vec_extras from "github.com/x/vec_extras@v2";`, and the
compiler checks it against the program's root as described above. The
library's own examples and tests are root files, so in them the line
declares the package, and the examples run on their own.

title: The native part
text:
A package can call a library installed on the machine or shipped beside the
program without compiling C of its own. An `extern "name" { ... }` block
declares functions to load from that shared library by name at program startup
(spec §7.10).

If the name produces the wrong library filename, map it in the sidecar's
`dylibs` list using a platform suffix, for example `dylibs_linux =
["SDL2=libSDL2-2.0.so.0"];`. A package supplies defaults for its own names. The
program's sidecar can override any of those names, with precedence determined
separately for each platform. Mapping a name that no block declares is an error.

A program that calls only these functions compiles and links no native code and
can run with `goose run` without a C toolchain. The rest of this section covers
packages that compile their own C.

A package can include headers in the program's generated C, so the C compiler
can inline small adapters into Goose functions:

```goose
// mylib.build
c_headers = ["include/adapters.h"];
```

Paths are relative to the package root, or the program's directory for its
own sidecar. As with `--include`, headers follow the generated types and
precede extern prototypes and function bodies. They can define `static inline`
implementations of `extern fn` declarations without a separate object file
or a command-line `--include`. Types from unimported modules are not available.
Headers must compile with the selected backend, including TinyCC for
`goose run`; a header-only package needs no external C toolchain for that mode.

`c_headers` takes the same platform suffixes as the other `c_*` lists. Headers
are included in list order: command-line `--include` entries, the program's
sidecar, then packages in load order. Headers include their own dependencies;
`c_include`, `c_defines` and `c_flags_*` still apply only to separately compiled
native sources, not the program's generated C.

The sidecar names the C in one of two ways. The first is plain sources,
which the compiler compiles with the given includes, defines, flags and
libraries:

```goose
// mylib.build
c_sources = ["src/mylib.c"];
c_include = ["include"];
c_libs_linux = ["m"];
```

The second is a CMake project at the package root, named by its static
library target:

```goose
// mylib.build
cmake_target = "mylib";
cmake_options = ["MYLIB_SIMD=ON"];
```

The compiler then configures and builds a small wrapper project around the
package's own CMakeLists and uses the target's complete link line, so a
package can be a thin Goose layer over an existing C library without any
CMake code written specifically for Goose. Submodules the package needs are
cloned with it. Either way, the native part is built once per C compiler
under `~/.goose/build`, and a program links it statically.

The functions that the package's `extern fn`s name must be defined by that
C (or by the C library); the runtime's own `gs_os_*` functions and similar
ones belong to the standard library. Every `.goose` file under the package
root belongs to the package, except files in a directory below the root
that has a sidecar of its own (such as an example program with its own C),
and files in the directories that the sidecar excludes:

```goose
// mylib.build
exclude = ["tools", "third_party/demo"];
```

Most values an `extern fn` passes have layouts that C can declare for
itself, such as a slice as `{ data, len }` (spec §7.10). A builder
(`T[>..]&`, such as `u8[>..]&`) is the exception: C appends to it through
the runtime's `gs_rref`, and `goose.h` gives separately compiled C access to
the runtime for this, along with `gs_bld_append` for bytes. The
compiler puts that header on the include path of every native part,
including the program's own and CMake targets, and rebuilds them all when
the header changes:

```c
#include "goose.h"
void mylib_name(gs_rref out, int64_t id) {   /* extern fn mylib_name(out: u8[>..]&, id: i64); */
    gs_bld_append(out, "item", 4);
}
```

A package's C is self-contained: two packages that must share C share a
repository, as `gfx`, `audio` and `ui` do. A package whose functions keep
one state for the process, or that may only be called from the main thread,
says so in its sidecar with `main_thread_only = true;`, and calling it from
a `thread_fn` is then a compile error.

title: Using Goose types in a C header
Files a package needs at run time
text:
`embed_file("path")` reads a file when the program is compiled (the path is
relative to the file containing the call) and gives its bytes as a
`const u8[:]` into static data, such as a font, a table or a shader source.
This is how a package ships data without having to deploy separate files.
Files read at run time belong to the program (`resource_dir()`,
`docs/stdlib.md`).

title: Publishing
text:
Push the repository, tag a version, and tell users the line to write:

```goose
import mylib from "github.com/you/mylib@v1";
```

There is no registry to register with. A tag can move and a branch always
does, so users who need a build to be reproducible pin a commit. Code from
a fetched package runs on the user's machine when its C is built, as with
any build script; pinning a version expresses trust in that code.

title: 5. The cache
text:
```
~/.goose/
  config                          cc = "clang";
  pkg/<host>/<owner>/<repo>/<ref>/   fetched packages, submodules included
  build/pkg/.../<toolchain>/      their native parts, per C compiler
  build/runtime/<hash>/...        the runtime object, per C compiler and configuration
  build/prog/<name>-<hash>/       each program's C, objects and logs
  toolchain/                      what finding the C compiler took (vcvars on Windows)
```

Deleting it loses nothing that a build cannot recreate.

title: Compiler and runtime tests
text:
> **Deprecated language features:** `reusable` and `reusable[]`. Use
> [`slot_pool<T>`](stdlib.md#slot_pool) for slots and
> [`slice_pool<T>`](stdlib.md#slice_pool) for contiguous runs.
> Builtin behavior and historical examples below remain relevant to existing
> code; removal is planned separately, after the remaining migration gaps.

title: Running the suite
text:
The deterministic language server test sends saved call hierarchy items
through `Server::Handle` directly after a document change. No background
analysis runs between the messages. Build and run it with:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build-lsp -DGOOSE_BUILD_LSP_TESTS=ON
cmake --build build-lsp --target goose_lsp_test --config Debug
ctest --test-dir build-lsp -C Debug -R lsp_call_hierarchy --output-on-failure
```

Run `python test/run_tests.py --profile baseline --cc native --require-clang`
after a normal compiler build. CI runs this on Windows, macOS and Linux.

The runners execute `-j`/`--jobs` jobs at once, defaulting to one per logical
processor up to 32. Their threads mostly wait for Goose, the C compiler, and the
programs they start. Each job buffers its output, and those buffers are printed
in job order. Logs therefore stay comparable regardless of the number of jobs.
`-j1` runs everything in order on one thread.

Runs of the same fixture are sequential because one run may write a file that
another would see (`stdlib_os.goose`, for example). The Goose-in-Goose chains
and sample runner start first. The sample runner (`samples/run_samples.py`) is a
separate process using the same number of jobs. The -O0 bootstrap chain is the
longest job, and the whole suite takes about as long as that chain.

`--gpu-jobs N` limits concurrent gfx programs within each runner for GPU drivers
that cannot handle many headless devices. There is no limit by default.

The log is divided into sections (parse, roundtrip and typecheck; generated
C; JIT runs; `errors_tc/`; samples; ...). Each section ends with a line
counting its checks, such as `== typecheck errors (...): 1668 ok`. Anything
a section prints other than its ok lines is shown in place, under the
section's title: a failure together with what led to it, and the skips. `-v`
also prints a line for every check that passed. Under GitHub Actions, those
ok lines are kept in a collapsed group per section, and the group is closed
before anything else prints. After the log, the FAIL lines are repeated with
the titles of their sections; under GitHub Actions they are printed as
annotations.

Each fixture is compiled as few times as its checks allow. One run of
`goose --roundtrip --check` parses the fixture, checks that its dump parses
again to the same dump, and typechecks it. That run adds `--bce-test` where
the fixture has annotations, uses `--parse` instead of `--check` for a
`parse-only` fixture, and adds `--dump-file` to write the dump for a
`dump-runtime` fixture. Each run has `--stats`, with which every run that
gets past resolution prints `parsed ok`, so a single `--check` of an `errors_tc/` fixture can tell a
parse failure from a typecheck failure. Where an optimization level both
builds the C and runs the program through TinyCC, one
`goose -O<n> --jit -o <file>` does both: it writes the C, then runs the
program in-process.

Most of those runs, and the runs of the `errors/` and `errors_tc/`
fixtures, share a compiler process with other fixtures.
`goose --multi-test <flags> a.goose b.goose ...` compiles each file in turn,
exactly as a separate run on that file would. It ends each file's part of
stdout and of stderr with a line `==== goose --multi-test: exit <code> <file>`.
From these lines the runner gives every fixture exactly the exit code and
output that a run of its own would have produced. Starting a compiler
process takes about as long as checking a small fixture, so a batch of 20 is
checked in a tenth of the time. If a batch crashes or aborts, the results for
the files before the one it was compiling are kept; that file and the rest
are then run one per process, so the crash is reported for the right
fixture. Runs that write a dump (`dump-runtime`), use `runtime-define`
defines, or run a program (TinyCC) still use one process each.

The C of the fixtures that do not link a native layer is also built a batch
at a time, at each optimization level and for the dump and `GS_DEBUG`
programs. One C compiler run compiles each program's unit with its `main`
renamed, together with a `main` that runs the program named by its first
argument, and links them once against the runtime object
(`CC.compile_programs` in `scripts/toolchain.py`). Every run of a program is
still a separate process. Where a batch does not build, each program in it
is built on its own, which shows why it failed. Starting and linking take
most of a C compiler run's time for these programs, so a batch of 20 builds
in a fifth of the time. `--batch N` sets how many files go to one compiler
process and how many programs go into one executable (by default, a number
that leaves every job some batches); `--batch 1` gives each file its own
process and each program its own executable.

title: Fixture layout
text:
Test fixtures are grouped by category; `run_tests.py` stays at the root of `test/`:

| Path under `test/` | Coverage |
|---|---|
| `syntax/` | Lexer, parser, dump grouping, imports and namespace resolution. Imported helpers live in `syntax/ns/` and `syntax/sub/`. `raw_strings_crlf.goose` is the only file checked out with CRLF line breaks (`.gitattributes`). |
| `typing/` | Types, generics, constants, optional narrowing, dispatch results and recursive return contracts. |
| `lifetimes/` | Reference roots, byte views, borrowed contents and shrinking while references are live. |
| `codegen/` | C names, evaluation order, representations, frame/stack layout and aliasing. |
| `optimizer/` | Inlining, tail recursion and bounds-check elimination. |
| `runtime/` | Runtime diagnostics, reusable slot and slice pool operations and array size checks, and `runtime_trim_memory.c`, the native test of releasing unused data-stack memory. |
| `storage/` | Relative references, pools and serialization. |
| `threads/` | Workers, queues, shared globals, contained workers' aborts and `runtime_threads_lifecycle.c`, the native runtime lifecycle test. Imported helpers live in `threads/spawn/`. |
| `stdlib/` | Standard-library modules. |
| `goose_in_goose/` | A Goose-written compiler used as one multi-file bootstrap regression: build and run three generations, check a C fixed point and repeated self-checks of the stage-2 compiler, and compare JIT/native self-compilation. |
| `audio/` | The `audio` module: the offline PCM mixer advanced by exact frame counts; the rejection of bad rates, PCM, parameters and output; voice and sound capacity and stale handles; and the threading rejection. |
| `gfx/` | The `gfx` graphics module: headless rendering, textures, compute, frames and input, a runtime misuse, shaders from files and from the program; shader and threading rejections (fixtures with `// error:` markers). The programs hold their shaders; the shader files beside them are for the file form of `embed_shader` and `--compile-shader`. |
| `physics/` | The `physics` module: worlds, bodies, every kind of shape and geometry, all joint kinds, queries, events, recording and replay, a runtime misuse, and the threading rejection. |
| `ui/` | The `ui` module: fonts, windows and layout, widgets, popups and menus, text editing, style, drawing and the input queries, charts, rendering and input through headless gfx, whether the keys and the mouse belong to the ui, a runtime misuse, the layer's misuse messages, and the threading rejection. |
| `packages/` | Programs declaring packages from path sources under `pkgs/`, built by `goose build`: pure Goose packages (`pkg_basic`), one with plain C under its sidecar (`pkg_c_lib`), a CMake one (`pkg_cmake_lib`, which `native_toolchain.py` also uses), and programs with C of their own from a sidecar (`pkg_own_c`; `pkg_float_abi`, floating-point arguments on the stack between native C and TinyCC). `pkgs/col` is the package `errors/pkg_collision.goose` imports. |
| `errors/`, `errors_tc/` | Expected parser/resolver and semantic rejections. |
| `errors_tc/recovery/` | Programs with several errors, which the parser, resolution and the checker continue past (`docs/design/language_server.md` §5 D). Taken in order, each `// error:` marker must be part of the message of the error at the same position in the order the compiler reports them, and there must be no other errors, both in text and under `--diagnostics json`. `imported/` holds a module that `imports.goose` imports, which is not a fixture of its own. |
| `lsp/` | Language-server fixtures driven by `lsp_protocol.py` over the protocol, not compiled as programs. `basics.goose` declares queries and expected answers in `// lsp:` lines and imports `helper.goose`. `complete.goose` ends with `p.` to test completion. `recovery.goose` has errors in two functions; `// lsp: error` lines specify their locations, and queries use the code checked so far. `broken_decls.goose` has errors inside a struct, an enum, and functions, plus an unresolved import. `exemplar.goose` tests queries on uncalled generic functions using exemplar checks (`docs/design/language_server.md` §11). `roots_lib.goose` contains an error and is opened and closed alongside its importers, `roots_app.goose` and `roots_app2.goose`. `source_index.goose` tests globals whose initializers omit defaults or expand a `const for`, a generic function matching a `const for` arm list, and calls containing commas in literals and comments. `two_a.goose` and `two_b.goose` import `two_shared.goose`; only the second instantiates its generic function. `ufcs_ns.goose` makes UFCS calls on a namespaced type from the global namespace, one of which matches no overload. `pools.goose` declares a root struct and uses a `slot_pool` and a `slice_pool`, whose generic functions taking the pool first must be offered as members. |
| `expected/` | Shared output and runtime-diagnostic expectations. |
| `run_tests.py` | The Python test runner. |
| `toolchain_selection.py` | Which compiler the runners use (`find_goose` in `scripts/toolchain.py`). An `--exe` path is used as given, made absolute, even when there are other compilers in `build/`. Without `--exe`, the runners use the first of `build/Release/`, `build/RelWithDebInfo/`, `build/` itself (for a single-configuration generator) and `build/Debug/`, so that a routine run uses an optimized compiler and an assertion build has to be chosen with `--exe`. If there is no compiler in any of these, or the `--exe` path does not exist, the run stops rather than using another compiler. A unittest, run by the main runner. |
| `compiler_roots.cpp` | Root-set join laws, feedback on weakening, order-independent equality and the deliberate comparison projections; compiled and run in both native profiles. |
| `compiler_containers.cpp` | The compiler's `small_vector` and `flat_map` against `std::vector` and `std::unordered_map` under random operations, across in-place/heap storage, growth and erasure, and `flat_map`'s reuse of an erased key's value cell; compiled and run in both native profiles. |
| `resource_paths.py` | Unicode source and C output paths, JIT entry-source resource roots, native executable roots with separate and standalone runtimes, relocation, and unchanged working-directory file access. Called by the main runner. |
| `cli_paths.py` | Tests command-line and import paths. `-o` may target a directory that does not yet exist, for generated C or a `goose build` executable. Package sources may be `"."` or `".."`, and an `--include` path may start with a separator. An unresolved import must report the searched locations or the absence of a standard library. Other cases pass a directory as the source or to `embed_file`, and run `--gen-runtime-header` without a source tree beside the compiler. Called by the main runner. |
| `extern_types.py` | One imported extern interface and C adapter with unused and partially used functions: slice, reference-pointee and return types are available to the header at O0/O2 through native C and TinyCC, with no implementation needed for an unused extern. Called by the main runner. |
| `extern_dylib.py` | An extern block bound from a shared library that the test builds. Every parameter shape goes through the runtime's binding, with the library opened by a spelling relative to the resource directory and by a bare name on the loader's path, both under the JIT (with no C toolchain available) and in a built program. The generated C is the same across compiles and binds only the members that are called. A missing library or symbol is a runtime error naming the spelling tried, and unused members need neither. A package declaring both kinds of extern builds its native part only for a program that calls its static one. The sidecar's `dylibs` lists map a name to the spelling each platform opens, with the program's mapping taking precedence over a package's, and a malformed entry or a name that no extern block declares is refused. Called by the main runner. |
| `runtime_cache.py`, `runtime_cache_cc.c` | Concurrent first builds share one completed runtime object; a failed compile cannot poison the cache, retry and reuse work, and dry runs leave the cache untouched. A controlled C compiler exercises both driver flag styles in debug and release configurations. Called by the main runner. |
| `native_toolchain.py` | A CMake interface package, runtime and program use one toolchain. Cache paths with and without spaces also exercise response-file arguments, using MinGW GCC on Windows when available. Called by the main runner. |
| `native_cache.py` | When several programs that use one package with C are built for the first time at once, that C is compiled only once. The other builds wait on the lock of the package's build directory and link the objects the first build made; the controlled C compiler of `runtime_cache_cc.c` checks that those objects are complete. A warm build compiles nothing. Both driver flag styles are tested. Called by the main runner. |
| `native_rebuild.py` | Tests when native code is rebuilt. Editing a program's C triggers rebuilding for `goose build` and `goose run`; naming the program by another path does not. Adding an extern fn without changing C rebuilds the JIT library. Other cases cover two C files with the same name in different directories, `--debug` and release builds side by side, and extern fns omitted from a library's symbol table. CMake tests cover reconfiguration after `cmake_options` changes, an undefined `cmake_target` reported during configuration, and a C++ target. Generated CMake files must keep their timestamps when unchanged, and a program's own CMake target must work regardless of how the program is named. Called by the main runner. |
| `native_builder.py` | C compiled on its own appends to a Goose builder: a `u8[>..]&` parameter arrives as `goose.h`'s `gs_rref`, and `gs_bld_append` adds bytes to it, from a program's sidecar C and from a CMake package's target, built by `goose build` and run in-process by `goose run`. Called by the main runner. |
| `runtime_io.py` | A program built by `goose build`, and run by `goose run` where the JIT runs, reads piped stdin: `read_stdin` gets every byte, a `\r\n` and a Ctrl-Z among them, which Windows' text mode would translate and stop at, and `read_line` into a builder already ending in a `\r` keeps that `\r`, and returns a line holding a NUL byte and a 70,000-byte line whole. On POSIX, `write_file_atomic` over a file keeps its permissions. Called by the main runner. |
| `commit_limit.py` | Windows only: a program running in a job object that limits its processes to committing 100 MB grows a data stack past that limit. The error must say that it is out of memory committing a data stack, not that the stack overran its reservation. Called by the main runner. |
| `huge_pages.py` | Linux only: the first 2 MB of each data stack region is marked for no transparent huge pages (`nh` in `/proc/<pid>/smaps`), so that a stack holding a few bytes commits a page rather than a huge one. Called by the main runner. |
| `exit_race.py` | The main program and eight workers write to stderr and call `exit(7)` at once, with the output redirected. Each of 20 runs of the program built by `goose build` must end with that exit code, even though on Windows two exits running the C library's teardown at the same time can crash it. Called by the main runner. |

Positive fixtures are discovered one level below `test/`; nested import helpers
run through their entry programs. `goose_in_goose/` is handled separately as one
bootstrap program, rather than discovering its modules as standalone fixtures.
Keep fixture stems unique across categories,
since expectations and generated build artifacts use those names. The runner
rejects duplicate names.

title: Configurations and backends
text:
| Configuration | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Debug Goose compiler; Goose `-O0` / native C `-O0` versus Goose `-O2` / native C `-O2` | Compare actual unoptimized and optimized executables, including native optimizer effects; check output against the existing fixtures. |
| Goose `-O2`, native C `-O2`, `GS_DEBUG=1`, selected fixtures | Exercise checked arithmetic/conversions and critical runtime paths with optimization enabled. Selection is `codegen_exec.goose` plus files with `runtime-debug` on their first line. |
| Additional Clang C build of `codegen_exec.goose`, native `-O1`, release/debug runtime; Clang builds of `simd_versions.goose`, `stdlib_base64.goose` and `simd_mul_add.goose`, native `-O2`, with `GS_SIMD=2`, `1` and `0`; Clang builds of `vec_elemwise.goose` with `GS_VEC=1` and `0` | Keep a second C-front-end check on the central codegen coverage file without repeating the whole suite for every backend. The `simd` functions' versions (spec §7.12) exist only where clang builds for x86-64: their C must contain every version, and at each level the C may be built for, the program must print what the baseline prints. `mul_add` is the exception. Run with `modes`, `simd_mul_add` reports the rounding of each kind of call: a plain function (once on arm64, twice on x86-64), and in a `simd` function a direct call, an `inline fn` helper, a plain helper and a function value. A direct call and a function value round once in the AVX2 and AVX-512 versions on a CPU with AVX2 and FMA; the helpers do too where Goose inlines them, and at Goose `-O0`, which inlines nothing, they round as the plain function does. The C is generated at both levels. The runner asks the operating system whether the CPU has them, and accepts either rounding where it can't ask. |
| Goose `-O0` and `-O2` through the in-process TinyCC backend, plus `GS_DEBUG=1` on the same selected fixtures, over every test and every sample | Check the generated C against a third, very different C implementation, and check that a program behaves the same whichever backend builds it. |
| One Linux Clang ASan/UBSan job | Instrument the C++ compiler, generated C, selected debug-runtime cases, all samples and the direct runtime tests (`runtime_threads_lifecycle.c`, `runtime_trim_memory.c`). |
| Goose-in-Goose bootstrap, both profiles | Build stage 1 with the real compiler, stage 2 with stage 1, and stage 3 with stage 2. Build all three executables, compare stage-2/stage-3 C, and run two self-checks in stage 2 while stage 3 is emitted and built (the fixed point makes stage 2 the same compiler as stage 3). The baseline profile requires the same self-compiled C across host/native O0 and O2 and across JIT/native execution; the sanitize profile instruments every native stage. |

Run just the bootstrap with
`python test/run_tests.py --goose-in-goose-only --exe <goose> --cc native`.
The usual `--profile`, `--no-jit`, and `--nocgen` options apply. With no native
C compiler, it still checks the source and, when available, self-compiles through
the JIT, but reports the native chain as skipped. Sources and the exact stage
contract are in [goose_in_goose/README.md](../test/goose_in_goose/README.md);
artifacts and logs go in `build/gen/<profile>/goose_in_goose/O<level>/`.

The sanitizer job builds Goose with
`-O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fno-sanitize-recover=all`,
then runs `python test/run_tests.py --exe <instrumented-goose> --profile sanitize --cc clang`.
Generated C uses native `-O1`, with UBSan's alignment check included for packed
accesses as well as for the C++ compiler. ASan observes C allocations, but does not
know logical object boundaries inside Goose's custom virtual-memory arenas.

Generated C is built as `goose -o` writes it, against the separate runtime
(`docs/implementation.md` §7). `GooseRuntime` (`scripts/toolchain.py`) has
the compiler under test write the runtime's C (`--emit-runtime`) once per
run. It compiles that C once per toolchain configuration (compiler,
optimization level, defines and extra flags, so the sanitize profile's
runtime is instrumented as well) into `build/gen/runtime/`, or for the
samples into their own directory. `CC.compile(..., runtime=...)` then links
that object with each program built this way. Stages 2 and 3 of the
bootstrap contain their own runtime and link none. Every TinyCC run compiles
the single-unit form, which `--standalone` writes; the benchmarks build that
form too.

The direct `test/threads/runtime_threads_lifecycle.c` regression checks allocations,
mappings and Windows handles across worker churn, including unjoined workers,
concurrent/repeated waits, children outliving their parents and contained
workers that abort. The direct `test/runtime/runtime_trim_memory.c` test
checks that releasing unused data-stack memory decommits the pages on
Windows and drops them from the resident set on Linux and macOS, while
keeping live partial pages and other stacks. It also checks that discarded
pages are zeroed, that Windows growth recommits through the fault handler
behind a commit mark that each trim moves, and that macOS growth needs no
runtime-handled faults, before or after a trim. Both run in both
profiles. The normal suite also checks
user-visible worker error diagnostics.

The `gfx/` tests exercise the gfx package (https://github.com/aardappel/goose_gfx,
its `docs/gfx.md`). They always parse, typecheck and generate C. When the
compiler includes the gfx layer (configured with the package,
`GOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS`), `goose build` links the tests against it and they run
at -O0 and -O2 and through TinyCC. They render headless into textures and
read back only pixel-aligned results, so their output is the same on every
backend and GPU. A machine with no GPU device (where the program prints
`gfx: no GPU device`) reports them as skipped, as does a compiler without
the layer. Linux CI runs them on Mesa's lavapipe. The runners set
`GOOSE_GFX_HEADLESS=1`, so no test or sample opens a window. The hidden
`--compile-shader` flag is tested on `gfx/probe.frag` and
`gfx/probe_badset.frag` in every compiler, with or without the layer
([Additional compiler checks](#additional-compiler-checks)).

The `physics/` tests exercise the physics package
(https://github.com/aardappel/goose_physics) in the same way. They always
generate C. When the compiler was configured with the package
(`GOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS`), `goose build` links them and they run at -O0 and
-O2 and through TinyCC. Box3D is deterministic across platforms and worker
counts, so the tests print rounded physics results and compare them exactly.
Together they call every function of the layer.

The `ui/` tests exercise the ui module of the gfx package (its `docs/ui.md`)
in the same way. `goose build` links the ui layer, and for the test that
renders through gfx, the gfx layer too. A test needs the layers of its own
category and of every module it imports, and is skipped where one of them is
not built into the compiler. The tests drive a context with their own input
and print what comes back and what was drawn; `ui_render` draws through
headless gfx and reads back pixels only where the ui drew solid color.
Together they call every function of the layer.

Each package's own `test/api_check.py` compares the functions, structs, and
constants in its modules with their C headers. This catches
interface mismatches that can compile successfully on both sides. It also
rejects a struct the layer passes by value that TinyCC would pass differently
from the C compilers on System V x86-64: a struct of at most 16 bytes that
has a misaligned field, or that has only floats in one eightbyte and
integers in the other.

The gfx package's own `test/window/run_window_test.py` (in
https://github.com/aardappel/goose_gfx) is run by hand, on a machine with a
display and a GPU. It uses the `scripts/toolchain.py` of a Goose checkout
(the sibling `goose` directory, or whatever `GOOSE_REPO` names). It runs the
showcase `gfx_showcase.goose` with a window, both in-process and built by
every C toolchain found, on each GPU driver of the platform. It checks what
the program reports about its own readbacks, and decodes the screenshots the
program saves (under the package's `build/gfx-window/`) to check them for
detail and compare them across runs.

The TinyCC runs are skipped under the sanitizers, because there the program
runs uninstrumented inside an instrumented compiler and still holds its
runtime allocations when that compiler exits. A test the backend cannot run
yet is reported as a skip, not a failure: either because the compiler
refuses the program (`JIT mode does not support`) or because the test's
first line says `no-jit`. Prefer portable assertions to skipping a backend;
the math tests allow small rounding differences in transcendental results.
See `docs/design/jit_backend.md` for the backend's remaining limitations and
possible solutions.

title: Expected output and diagnostics
text:
An explicitly requested compiler must exist; CI does not silently skip it.
Every runnable fixture requires an `expected/<name>.out`, including an empty
file when the program should be silent. Expected aborts additionally require
`.aborts` and a nonempty `.stderr` containing the expected runtime diagnostic
substrings. Sanitizer reports fail even when a program was expected to abort.
Resource-bound fixtures can set a limit in their first line, such as
`// runtime-define: GS_MAX_STACKS=1`. The runner passes it as a `-D` to
every compile: the compiler checks `GS_MAX_STACKS` against the program's
static stack count, and the generated C takes care of the rest. Fixtures
that use this:

* `append_destination_storage.goose` detects temporary result stacks that
  output-only comparisons would miss.
* `cycle_scratch_locals.goose` shows that a recursion's scratch locals use
  the same few stacks at every level.
* `discarded_resizable_results.goose` shrinks each stack's reservation
  (`GS_STACK_RESERVE`) so that its loops overflow a stack unless every
  discarded result is released. `guard_flat_storage.goose` does the same for
  what a guard's condition, its else and the rest of its block use on the
  data stacks (the rest of the block is emitted without braces of its own).
  `continue_restores.goose` and `large_fixed_exits.goose` do the same for
  the watermarks that a `continue`, a `break` and a `return ... from`
  restore.
* `thread_cap.goose` shrinks the address space budget (`GS_STACK_BUDGET`)
  so that `hardware_threads()` reports its minimum of one wherever it runs.
* `stack_stats.goose` has its program report its stack use
  (`GS_STACK_STATS`), which is checked through
  `expected/stack_stats.stderr`.

`cycle_static_stacks.goose` runs the shapes that a call into a recursive
cycle allows (§7.8); the `errors_tc/cycle_temporary_*`,
`cycle_construction_*` and `cycle_result_*` fixtures are the rejected
shapes. Codegen fails with an internal error if any program holds a data
stack across such a call. The runner also checks the shape, but not the
counts, of the `--stacks` report of `thread_cap.goose` and
`cycle_scratch_locals.goose`. For `thread_spawn_discarded.goose`, whose
worker holds no regions, it checks that the report gives no thread cap. A
fixture expecting a debug-only abort sets `GS_DEBUG=1` the same way, which
makes every run of it a debug build: `cast_abort_location.goose` and
`overflow_abort_location.goose` check the location that a failing check
reports, and `thread_contained.goose` checks that the debug checks end only
the contained worker.

Parser/resolver errors live in `test/errors/`; semantic errors live in
`test/errors_tc/` and must get past parsing and resolution (`parsed ok`)
before they fail. Each source declares one or
more `// error: <diagnostic substring>` lines. The compiler must exit with 1,
and every marker must occur in one of these: diagnostic headers,
`in const for` expansion context lines, the instantiation chain's `in fn`
lines (without their ` instantiated from <path>:<line>` part), or the
reasons on overload candidates' lines. Echoed source does not count. The
compiler continues past the errors it can recover from, so a fixture may
print more errors than it declares; `test/errors_tc/recovery/` holds the
fixtures that declare all of their errors, in order (see the table above).
In a marker, use the specific rejection reason and relevant types/roots;
omit source paths, line numbers and specification section numbers.
`errors_tc/function_value_chain.goose` names a block's file, line and column
on purpose, because what it checks is how the chain names a block. These
inline assertions replace the old compiler-error `.stderr` files.

A fixture declares the warnings its `--check` prints in the same way, with
one `// warning: <message substring>` line per warning; a positive fixture
that declares none must print none. Markers and warning lines are paired one
to one, and each marker must be part of the message of a different warning
line. So a warning printed twice fails the fixture, just as a missing or an
undeclared warning does (a warning is printed once for its node as written
in the source, `docs/implementation.md` §3.12). Two `&`s on one line that
produce the same warning print two identical lines and need two markers, as
`r6` in `branch_reference_copies.goose` does. The order of the markers does
not matter. Without line numbers, a marker could not say where a warning is,
and warnings print in the order in which checking reaches their nodes: a
callee's body at its first call, a loop's or a construct's once its checks
settle, and redundant casts by line after the whole program. A change to the
checker may rearrange that order without changing what a program is told.
The warnings of a rejection test are checked only if it declares some:
checking stops at its error, so which warnings are printed first depends on
how far checking got. For example, `cycle_local_store.goose` warns about its
recursive call's `&local` before the error that the call reveals, at the
store on the line above.

title: Additional compiler checks
text:
The runner checks more than exit status and runtime output:

| Check | Contract |
|---|---|
| `lexer_tokens.goose` | Exact token stream, including keyword classification, decoded literals and longest-match punctuation. |
| Every positive Goose fixture | Successful parse, successful initial dump, identical dump/reparse/dump, and typechecking with exactly the warnings it declares, unless its first line contains `parse-only`. Parsing also resolves type names; dumping alone does not. |
| First-line `dump-runtime` | Compile and execute the dumped source against the original output. `control_expression_dump.goose` uses this to check grouping semantics, which a stable dump alone cannot establish. |
| Every fixture with `// bce:elide` or `// bce:keep` | Run `-O1 --check --bce-test`, including expected-abort regressions. Native/JIT O0 and O2 runs independently check behavior. |
| `gfx_err_shader_syntax.goose`, `gfx_err_shader_part.goose` | Besides their markers, the error is reported at the program's line holding the offending GLSL. |
| `gfx/probe.frag`, `gfx/probe_badset.frag` | `goose --compile-shader`, the shader compiler that every compiler has, with or without the gfx layer. `probe.frag` compiles, including its `#include` of `probe_common.glsl`, and reports its one sampler and its 32-byte uniform block. `probe_badset.frag`, which has a sampler outside the set that SDL_GPU gives a fragment shader's textures, is rejected with the rule it broke. |
| Generated `call_chain.goose`, `call_chain_too_deep.goose` (`build/gen/<profile>/`) | A compile-time call path through 2000 distinct functions passes the check at `-O0` and runs through TinyCC. At `-O2`, where the inliner may fold its single-use functions into one body only 64 C blocks deep at a time, it builds with the native C compiler and runs (`docs/implementation.md` §4). A path through 6000 functions, each calling the next from 32 blocks deep, is rejected as too deep for the compiler's stack instead of overflowing it (§3.1). |
| Generated `guard_runs.goose` (`build/gen/<profile>/`) | 300 guards in a row, in a function's body and in a loop's body, build with the native C compiler and run at `-O0` and `-O2`: the rest of the block after a guard whose else leaves the block opens no C block (`docs/implementation.md` §6.2). This matters because MSVC stops at 128 nesting levels and clang at 256.
