A chain of 200 single-use functions, each calling the next behind four guards, folds at `-O2` into bodies 64 blocks deep, which would nest past both limits if the inliner's count left out blocks codegen opens (§4). |
| `loop_shapes.goose` at O1 | Read the generated C: every `shape_` function has the restated loop it is named for, marked by codegen's `/* loop shape: ... */` comment, and no `keep_` function has one (`docs/implementation.md` §6.12). Its runs check that each restated loop computes what a reference loop does. |
| `member_parameters.goose` at O1 | Read the generated C: `walk`, which takes two slices and a `T[>..]&`, has each as two scalar C parameters (data pointer and count, header pointer and stack; spec C.3, `ParamFields`). Its runs pass slices, builders and pool references through calls, a recursion, a case-function dispatch, nested functions' free variables, a `simd` function, a `format` overload and an exported wrapper. |
| `member_stores.goose` at O1 | Read the generated C: `store_links` stores to fields reached through references that cannot be rebound, with no index on the way, as C member stores rather than through a pointer taken first (`StableDest`). Its runs check the stores, and check that when the right side rebinds the reference, the store still goes to the destination named before the right side ran (`evaluation_order.goose` has a right side writing the destination itself). |
| `optimize.goose` at O0/O1/O2 | Inspect named tail-recursion bodies in `--specs`: supported integer accumulator and plain recursion become loops, including a list walk that hands on a node read through its parameter. Modulo, floating-point reassociation, nonlocal-return frames, returns inside nested loops and a reference to a local passed down keep their self calls. Mixed operators retain the ineligible call. Leading locals prevent base-case inlining from consuming these cases first. The `gb_` functions count the copies of their first statement: guarded base-case inlining copies the body once per self-call site where the test compares unassigned parameters, including self-calls written with UFCS, but not where the test reads a global or a node, does arithmetic, or reads an assigned parameter. A u64 above i64.max that the optimizer creates (here, the starting accumulator of a fold and of `tre_and`) dumps as that unsigned value. |
| `optimize.goose` at O1, its C | `il_pair`, an `inline fn` returning two values, stays a call in Goose but is declared `GS_INLINE` in the C, for the C compiler to inline (spec §7.13). `il_plain`, a copy of `il_big` without the keyword, is not. |
| `docs/reference.md` | Every ```` ```goose ```` block of the language reference compiles (as written, or wrapped in a `main`), a block marked `// error` fails, no block warns, and where the JIT runs, each complete program prints what the block after it shows. `scripts/check_doc_examples.py` does the work in a process of its own, as the samples' runner does, writing the blocks under `build/gen/<profile>/doc_examples/`; its docstring has the markers a document uses for a block that is only a fragment or is compiled without being run. Run it by hand on any document: `python scripts/check_doc_examples.py docs/reference.md --run -v`. |
| The command line (`driver_verbs` in `run_tests.py`) | The verbs against the flags they stand for: `goose run` (where the JIT runs) prints what the program does, `goose check` only checks it, and `goose run -o` is refused; `goose version` and `goose --version` print the compiler's version and the runtime's 12 hex digits; a word that is not a command, an option or a file is an unknown command, named with the command it is close to; `--color always` and `CLICOLOR_FORCE` color an error and its caret, and output that is not a terminal, or `NO_COLOR`, has none; `goose check` prints nothing on success, and with `--stats` its `typechecked ok` line; every shell's completion script names the commands and their options, bash's (where there is bash) completes a command, an option and a `.goose` file, and zsh's parses (where there is zsh); `goose help --man` holds every command's help, and groff (where there is one) reads it without a warning; a `--stack-reserve` under 64 KB is refused. For the help: `goose --help` names the commands but not the hidden flags; together, `goose <command> --help` for run, build, check, fetch, format, toolchain, version, lsp and completion, `goose help c` and `goose help internals` name every option that `src/main.cpp` reads except the hidden shader ones; `goose help build` names `--dry-run`; an unknown topic is refused; and no file, or `goose build` with none, prints the usage. `goose toolchain --json` finds a C compiler wherever the runner found one, escapes a tab in `GOOSE_HOME`, and does not mistake a directory named `git` on PATH for git; with no C compiler anywhere, `goose toolchain` names every one it looked for; and `goose build --cc` naming a file that is not a program says why it cannot start it. Where there is a C compiler, `goose build` builds an executable that runs, and `--dry-run` prints what it would run without building one. |
| `doc_comments.py` | `goose --dump-docs` prints the documentation comments of a program's declarations, fields and variants: the run of `//` lines directly above each one, without its indentation. A blank line, a block comment or any token ends a run, a comment after code does not start one, and a banner followed by a blank line belongs to nothing. The program still checks and roundtrips. |
| `format.py` | `goose format`: each golden case, formatted through standard input, prints the layout it expects and is a fixed point. The cases cover the spaces the parser's token roles decide (unary against binary operators, generic lists against comparisons, type suffixes, `as!`, `[>..<]`, ranges), trailing commas added where a list's closing bracket starts a line and not after an initializer list's `..`, an array's fill form, parentheses or a last match arm ending in `return` or a bare `break`, a run of declarations lined up in columns, indentation (tabs, continuations keeping their offset from the line they continue and going no further left than it, so that a chain broken after its operators stays lined up under its first operand, bracket-aligned lines moving with their bracket, the body of a wrapped header or condition, `})`), blank lines, `\r\n` and a byte order mark, trailing comments moved with their line and aligned runs kept aligned, block comments and a multi-line string moved with their line, and a table of statements after semicolons kept. The command line: a file rewritten in place, a formatted one left with its modification time, `--check` listing what is not formatted (exit 1) and writing nothing, the directory walk (`.goose` files, sorted, no dot-directories or build trees unless named), a file that does not parse left as it is while the others are formatted (exit 2, which wins over `--check`'s 1), a read-only file refused, standard input with no files or `-`, wrong arguments, `--verify` and the help. A file's documentation comments come through as `--dump-docs` printed them. A second task, `format_sweep`, runs `goose format --verify` over `samples/`, `stdlib/`, `bench/` and `test/`: every file must format, pass the formatter's own checks (the same tokens and comments, a comma added only before a closing bracket, a parse to the same dump and documentation) and come out the same when formatted again; the only files skipped as not parsing must be under `errors/` or `errors_tc/`, or be the four fixtures broken on purpose. |
| `lsp_protocol.py` | Drives `goose lsp` over its protocol to check editor queries, diagnostics, edits, error recovery, root changes, and queries spanning multiple programs. See [Language server protocol checks](#language-server-protocol-checks) below. Before the first client's shutdown, `textDocument/formatting` of an unsaved document with `\r\n` line breaks returns edits that turn its text into what `goose format -` prints and touch only the lines that change; a formatted document gets no edits, and one that does not parse, or one not open, null. |
| `packages_git.py` | Besides the fetches, `goose check --offline` rejects a package not in the cache at its import, naming `goose fetch`, without fetching, and accepts it once fetched. |
| `diagnostics_json.py` | `goose check --diagnostics json` prints an array with one object per error or warning, whose `text` is what text mode prints on stderr; the progress lines go to stderr instead of stdout. A lexer error is placed at its caret's column, one byte wide, and the errors after a `"""` string that the lexer rejected are placed at their own lines. A typecheck error's range covers the node it is reported at, and its instantiation chain's entries are placed at the calls they name. A warning has a range too. An import error covers the whole import. A `checkfree` function's kept checks are reported as several errors at once. An error with no place in the program has only its text. |

title: Language server protocol checks
text:
`lsp_protocol.py` first runs `--probe`. A client in the runner then initializes
the server with `test/lsp/basics.goose` as its entry file and the VS Code
extension's commands. It opens the file, waits for diagnostics (there should be
none), and sends the queries specified by its `// lsp:` lines. These check:

* Hover text; definitions at a position, in a file, or absent; document symbols;
  and signature help with the active parameter.
* Semantic token types at a position, including positions with no token; reference
  counts; and renames that either make the expected number of edits or are refused.
  Each rename edit must change only the name's leaf.
* Inlay hint text, position, and count per line. Defaults inserted by the checker
  must produce no hints. Folding ranges must cover the expected lines, and
  selection-range chains must contain the requested range and be nested.
* Code-lens positions and titles. An instantiation lens must have a count matching
  its data lines and the command that lists them. A "Run" lens must carry the
  file's URI; "not instantiated" must be a title alone.
* Completion labels that must be present or absent, and text an item's detail
  must hold. `complete.goose` ends with `p.`, as source often does when an
  editor requests completion.
* Incoming and outgoing calls, including the function at the other end and the
  call lines. Uncalled functions must have no call results, and names that are
  not functions must have no call item.
* A workspace symbol from the imported `helper.goose`.

The test also checks that analysis asks the client to refresh code lenses,
semantic tokens, and inlay hints. It then checks the following changes and
additional roots in order:

1. A burst of edits introduces an error and removes it. Diagnostics must reflect
   the latest text, and a change must cancel an interrupted analysis. The test then
   inserts a line at the top and immediately requests a hover at the shifted
   position. The answer must use the new text. An incremental edit (a range plus
   its fragment, as a client with incremental sync sends) inserts a comment line
   above the file: the hint below it must stand, shifted down a line.
2. `recovery.goose` and `broken_decls.goose` are opened as separate roots. Every
   error must be published, and queries must still receive answers. Document
   symbols requested immediately after opening `recovery.goose` must come from its
   analysis, rather than return an empty result.
3. `source_index.goose` checks that global initializers are indexed as written,
   even though the checker rewrites them in place. Bindings in `const for` arms
   must resolve, and signature help must ignore commas in literals and comments.
   `ufcs_ns.goose` checks that signature help, and hover and definitions on a
   resolved call and on one that matches no overload, find a UFCS call's
   functions in the namespace of its receiver's type, not the global ones.
4. `errors_tc/recovery/inside_braces.goose` checks errors inside struct-literal and
   match braces. They must appear at their source locations, with no extra errors.
5. `exemplar.goose` and `errors_tc/recovery/exemplar_unchecked.goose` check queries
   on uncalled generic functions through their exemplars. In the second file,
   those bodies must produce no diagnostics even though no binding could make them
   correct. Its only error is in main, as reported by `goose check`.
6. Roots are opened, closed, and edited. After a request runs the due analyses,
   the test checks the last diagnostics published for each file. It opens
   `roots_lib.goose`, which contains an error, alone and then alongside its
   importer `roots_app.goose`. Closing that importer must leave hover and document
   symbols available again. Next it opens both `roots_app.goose` and
   `roots_app2.goose` as importers, then edits the first to stop importing the
   library. The library's error must appear at every step, only once when both
   roots import it. Separately, `helper.goose` stays open while `basics.goose`
   closes and ceases to be an entry file. The helper's hover must then use its own
   root analysis.

The first server shuts down cleanly. A second client starts with `two_a.goose`
and `two_b.goose` as entry files. It renames a function in their shared import,
`two_shared.goose`, then requests references and incoming calls. Results must
include both programs, with each location listed once. They must also include
callers of a function reached only by the second program's instantiation of a
generic function. The second server then shuts down.

Run `test/lsp_sweep.py` by hand; it is separate from the main runner. It
measures `goose lsp` robustness and latency across every sample, the
goose_in_goose bootstrap, every stdlib module, and all positive, `errors/`, and
`errors_tc/` fixtures.

For each program, it opens a separate root and waits for diagnostics. At every
identifier start and after every `.`, it requests hover, definition, completion,
and signature help, plus incoming and outgoing calls for any function named
there. It requests semantic tokens, symbols, folding, inlay hints, and code
lenses once per program. It then makes ten random one-character edits in a burst
and waits for diagnostics. After restoring the text, it checks that diagnostics
match the initial ones.

The sweep fails if the server exits, returns an error, takes over 2 s for a
request, or stops responding. It prints the slowest files and requests.
`--quick` checks a handful of files in a second or two. The baseline is in
`docs/design/language_server.md` §12.

title: Fixture audit
text:
A fixture is load-bearing when some regression would fail it and nothing
else. Two fixtures with similar diagnostics are not necessarily duplicates:
they can exercise different expression visitors, specialization/cache states,
root propagation, or generated layouts. Whole-program globals and call graphs
are also part of many regressions, so combining two fixtures can change the
property under test.

The October 2026 audit measured this. It ran the suite with a compiler built
with clang's `-fsanitize-coverage=trace-pc-guard` and with an instrumented
runtime object, and recorded, for every fixture, the compiler edges its runs
hit and the runtime lines its programs ran. Coverage was counted only toward
fixtures that would notice the same regression:

* a positive fixture's coverage toward other positive fixtures (a rejection
  does not notice the checker refusing a good program);
* a bce-annotated fixture's coverage in `bce.h` toward other annotated
  fixtures;
* a rejection's coverage in the checker's files toward other rejections of
  the same rule (a program accepted by mistake goes unnoticed by positive
  fixtures and by other rules' rejections).

No fixture's coverage was fully contained in that of any single other fixture.
Even when coverage overlaps, a fixture may catch a failure that others miss. A
fixture covered entirely by the rest of its class was therefore removed only if
all of these conditions held:

* Named fixtures checked the same behavior through the same construct.

* It had not been added later as a regression test for a bug those fixtures
  missed.

* It checked nothing that coverage alone cannot show, such as an expected
  runtime diagnostic, an integer width or extreme value, a `GS_DEBUG` check, or
  output text.

A second review challenged every proposed removal. All removals together also
had to preserve each class's coverage.

This removed 153 `errors_tc/` fixtures and two positive ones. Most of the
removed `errors_tc/` fixtures tested a shrink, store or provenance rule
reached through the same construct as a sibling. The two positive ones were
`threads/thread_spawn_bound.goose`, whose generic thread_fn bindings
`thread_spawn_modules.goose` spawns through the same generics with checked
output, and `typing/fill_counts.goose`, whose computed fill counts
`named_const_readonly_refs.goose`, `appended_literals.goose` and
`const_name_scopes.goose` build and print. Nearly every positive candidate
stayed: most abort with a diagnostic that no other fixture's `.stderr` pins,
or pin values, types or output that run the same compiler edges. Small
fixtures on one subject were merged. Each original fixture became a function
of its own, called in the original order, and the expected output is their
outputs concatenated:

| Fixture | Merged from |
|---|---|
| `codegen/adt_field_tags.goose` | `variable_adt_field_tag.goose`, `resizable_adt_tail_tag.goose` |
| `codegen/relative_optional_null.goose` | `relative_null_tests.goose`, `relative_optional_targets.goose` |
| `codegen/named_result_destinations.goose` | `named_result_bytes.goose`, `named_result_exclusions.goose`, `inlined_named_result_tail.goose` |
| `lifetimes/shrink_operand_values.goose` | `shrink_owned_copies.goose`, `shrink_fresh_receivers.goose`, `shrink_argument_values.goose` |
| `lifetimes/break_value_roots.goose` | `break_value_provenance.goose`, `break_value_holder_contents.goose` |
| `storage/relative_default_values.goose` | `relative_defaults.goose`, `relative_default_fields.goose` |
| `storage/serialize_image_checks.goose` | `serialize_canonical.goose`, `serialize_offset_overflow.goose` |
| `syntax/extern_block_dump.goose` | `extern_block.goose`, `extern_block_escapes.goose` |
| `optimizer/basecase_aliased_guards.goose` | `basecase_reference_alias.goose`, `basecase_slice_alias.goose` |
| `optimizer/tail_reference_params.goose` | `tail_reference_rebind.goose`, `tail_reference_read.goose` |
| `runtime/float_text_digits.goose` | `float_text_f64.goose`, `float_text_shortest.goose` |
| `runtime/float_conversions_unchecked.goose` | `f32_casts_unchecked.goose`, `f64_conversions_unchecked.goose` |
| `typing/variable_size_literals.goose` | `variable_element_literals.goose`, `variable_literal_equality.goose` |
| `typing/nested_fn_assignments.goose` | `nested_fn_exits_assigned.goose`, `nested_fn_reused_assigns.goose` |
| `typing/type_aliases.goose` | `alias_nominal_recursion.goose`, `variant_aliases.goose` |
| `typing/dispatch_result_no_reference.goose` | `dispatch_result_diverging_case.goose`, `dispatch_result_null_case.goose` |
| `typing/constant_widths.goose` | `constant_extents.goose`, `constant_shift_wrap.goose` |

The audit also compared each rejection's comment with the error it reports.
Where a later rule caught a fixture first, the fixture was changed to reach
the rule it names. Where its old program was the only test of the path it
did reach, that program was kept as a separate fixture named for that path.
For example, the `growshrink_reach_*` fixtures hold a second root, so that
the caller's storage only bounds what they store, beside the
`growshrink_exact_*` ones, whose holders' contents are known exactly;
`index_type_let_array.goose` and `index_type_fixed_array.goose` pin the two
halves of the index-type array rule; and the `fnval_*` fixtures are named
for the function-value rule they reach. Markers that any rejection of their
kind would match (`cannot clear`, `read-only`, a type name) were replaced by
the specific message. Markers may also match the instantiation chain's frames
and an overload candidate's reason, which some fixtures exist to pin.

The small `return_from_cycle.goose` remains beside `return_from_cached_call.goose`:
the former checks replay through a recursion back edge without an additional
cached-call path, which could otherwise mask a missing propagation step.

CI uses four jobs to cover these configurations without testing every
combination of platform, sanitizer, optimization level, and runtime mode.
Benchmarks run separately from CI.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Goose for C++ and Rust Programmers: Translating Common Patterns
text:
Oct 22, 2026 · @Ben

Most C++ and Rust code translates to Goose once you stop asking "where do I allocate this?" and start asking "which scope owns this, and what array does it live in?" This guide takes patterns you already write daily and shows the Goose shape of each, with the reason it differs.

It is drawn from the official [tutorial](https://aardappel.github.io/goose/docs/tutorial.html), [language reference](https://aardappel.github.io/goose/docs/reference.html), [standard library](https://aardappel.github.io/goose/docs/stdlib.html) and design notes. The examples use syntax shown in those documents; check the reference when something does not compile. Most examples assume `import std;` at the top of the file (for `trim`, `split`, `sort`, `filter`, `remove_at` and friends), and the `dictionary` examples also need `import dictionary;`.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: The one shift: memory is a few stacks
text:
Goose has no `malloc`, no `free`, no GC, no reference counting and no destructors. Memory is the native stack plus a handful of **data stacks** the compiler sizes for your program. Four rules follow, and almost every pattern below is a consequence of them:

1. **Every dynamic value is owned by a variable.** A local, a global, a by-value parameter, or a field or element of one. Nothing floats free on a heap.
2. **Scope exit is the free.** When the owning scope ends, the stack pointer moves back. One store, no walk, no destructors.
3. **Nothing moves.** A growable array is always the top of its own stack, so `push` never reallocates. A reference into it stays valid after a million pushes, which a `Vec` or `std::vector` cannot promise.
4. **Values nest inline.** A string inside a struct inside an array is bytes inside bytes inside bytes, with no pointers between them.

The compiler proves all of it statically. There are no lifetime annotations; references carry an inferred *root* (the variable that owns their target) and may not outlive it.

On top of that, the type system is closed-world: no inheritance, no traits, no vtables, no function pointers, no escaping closures. Dynamic polymorphism is algebraic data types and nothing else.

**How to read this guide.** Each section names the C++/Rust habit, shows it, then shows the Goose version. The quick reference table right below is the index.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Quick reference
text:
| You write in C++ / Rust | You write in Goose | Section |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `new T`, `make_unique`, `Box::new` | A local, or `push` into an array that outlives you | Heap allocation |
| `vector<T>`, `Vec<T>` | `T[>..]` (grow-only); `T[>..<]` if you pop | Containers |
| `string`, `String` | `u8[>..]` builder; `u8[]` finished; `u8[..16]` inline | Containers |
| `string_view`, `&str`, `span`, `&[T]` | `T[:]` slice (checked, can't dangle) | Containers |
| `x.clone()`, copy constructor of a vector | `copy(x)`, always explicit | Heap allocation |
| Virtual method, `dyn Trait` | `enum` + `match`, or case functions | Virtual functions |
| `vector<unique_ptr<Base>>` | `Shape[>..]` (fixed mode) or `Shape..[>..]` (packed) | Virtual functions |
| Trait bound, C++ concept | Untyped / `<T>` generic, checked per instantiation | Traits |
| `impl Hash for K`, `operator<<` | A free `hash(k: K)` or `format(out, v: K)` overload | Traits |
| Methods, `impl` blocks | Free functions; `x.f(a)` is `f(x, a)` | Traits |
| `std::function`, stored `Box<dyn Fn>` | Compile-time function value; stored behaviour becomes an enum tag | Callbacks |
| `Box<Node>` tree, `Vec<Node>` + `u32` indices | `Node[>..]` pool + `Node&<u32>?` links | Linked structures |
| `shared_ptr`, `Rc<RefCell<T>>`, object pool | `slot_pool<T>` from the standard library + `alloc_ref` / `free` | Non-nested lifetimes |
| Struct owning three `Vec`s | A `root struct` whose three fields grow independently | Structs that own several vectors |
| `Result<T, E>`, `?`, `throw` | Trailing `bool`, `T?`, `return E from f`, `exception::try` | Errors |
| RAII destructor | Scope exit (memory); explicit `release` (external handles) | RAII |
| `Arc<Mutex<T>>`, `std::thread` + shared data | `thread_fn` + typed queues of flat values | Threads |
| serde, protobuf | `to_bytes` / `from_bytes<T>` / `bytes_of` | Serialization |
| `std::optional<T&>`, `Option<&T>`, `nullptr` | `T?`, narrowed by `if` / `guard` | Smaller habits |
| `std::tuple`, `(a, b)` returns | `-> A, B` multiple results (no tuple type) | Smaller habits |

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Heap allocation: there is no heap
text: In C++ and Rust you allocate when a value's size is dynamic or when it must outlive the current call. In Goose the first case is just a local, and the second is a value returned by value or pushed into an array owned further up.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: "I need a buffer of runtime size"

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: "I build something and hand it back"

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: "I need my own copy"
text:
Fixed-size values (scalars, structs of fixed fields, `T[k]`, references, slices) copy silently on `=`, like C. Anything whose size isn't known at compile time **never copies implicitly**: `let b = a;` binds `b` to `a` by reference. You write `copy(a)` to get an O(n) copy, so every expensive copy is visible in the source.

```
var a: i64[>..] = [1, 2, 3];
let alias = a;        // same array
var mine = copy(a);   // independent
```

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: "The object must outlive this function"
text: The question becomes *which scope should own it*. Usually the answer is a caller: the caller declares the array and passes it down as `T[>..]&`; the callee pushes into it and gets back a reference from `push`. When no scope fits because lifetimes truly interleave, use a `reusable` pool (see Non-nested lifetimes).

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Containers and strings: pick the array by what its size does
text:
There is no single `vector`. The array family differs only in what happens to the size, and every member stores `[metadata][elements]` inline with no pointer to a separate block.

| You want | C++ / Rust | Goose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A growable list you keep references into | `vector<T>` / `Vec<T>` (references invalidated on growth) | `T[>..]` grow-only: the default |
| A stack, queue or heap | `vector` + `pop_back`, `BinaryHeap` | `T[>..<]` grow-shrink, with `heap_push` / `heap_pop` from `std` |
| A small bounded list inside a struct | `std::array` + count, `ArrayVec`, `SmallVec` | `T[..k]` (fixed-size, inline) |
| Built once, then read-only | `vector` you stop touching, `Box<[T]>` | `T[]` or `T[varint]` |
| Compile-time size | `std::array<T, N>`, `[T; N]` | `T[k]` |
| A view of someone else's elements | `span<T>`, `&[T]` | `T[:]` |

Two rules shape how you use them. At most one *resizable* value (`T[>..]` or `T[>..<]`) may sit in a struct, and only as its last field. And an array's elements may not themselves be resizable.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: `vector<string>` and `Vec<String>`
text:
```
var words: u8[][>..] = [];
for i in 5 { words.push(str("word", i)); }
```

This is one contiguous block: a count, then five `(length, bytes)` runs. No per-string allocation, no pointer per element. The cost is that variable-size elements make the array **sequential**: you can iterate it but not index it (`words[2]` is a compile error).

If you need to index or sort, make each element fixed-size with an inline capacity:

```
var names: u8[..16][>..] = [];   // each name up to 16 bytes, indexable, sortable
```

Or keep the compact array and an index of references beside it (Linked structures shows this).

title: String building (`ostringstream`, `format!`, `String::push_str`)

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Erasing from the middle, retaining, dedup
text: These are library functions taking the array by reference: `remove_at`, `swap_remove`, `insert_at`, `retain`, `dedup`. A grow-only array may shrink only where the compiler can see nothing still points into it; if you hold a slice into it that is used later, the call is rejected and the error names the slice.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Virtual functions and trait objects become enums
text: Goose has no inheritance, no traits and no vtables. Its only runtime polymorphism is the `enum` (an algebraic data type). That covers the overwhelmingly common case: a known, closed set of kinds that you store together and act on uniformly.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Visitor pattern, double dispatch
text: A visitor exists to fake pattern matching, so it disappears: write the `match`. For double dispatch (collide A with B), nest two matches, or write a case-function set whose body matches on the second argument. Case-function dispatch happens on one parameter position.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Generic code over every variant
text: If you would reach for a derive macro or reflection ("print every variant's fields"), use `const for <N, V> in variants<T>` and `const for <F, A> in fields<V>`, which expand at compile time into ordinary code.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Traits, concepts and methods become overloads and generics
text: Static polymorphism in Goose works like C++ templates without concepts: a generic body is checked only at each concrete instantiation, and everything is monomorphized. There are no trait bounds to declare. What a trait or a concept would *name*, you provide as an overload of a free function.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Generic functions
text:
```
fn twice(x) { x + x }                         // an untyped parameter is generic
fn span<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T { if a > b { a - b } else { b - a } }   // <T> says a and b agree
fn zero<T>() -> T { default<T>() }           // explicit type arg when nothing infers it
let half = zero<f64>() + 0.5;
```

A type parameter is always a type, never a size: `fn f<N>(a: i64[N])` is an error. Take a slice `T[:]` instead, which every array kind converts to.

Errors appear at the instantiation, with the call chain that produced it, much like a C++ template error but with the chain spelled out.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: `impl Hash for MyKey`, `std::hash<MyKey>`
text:
Write a `hash` overload. `dictionary` finds it by overload resolution.

```
struct key { a: i64, b: i64 }
fn hash(k: key) -> u64 { hash_combine(hash(k.a), hash(k.b)) }

var seen = dictionary<key, bool> {};    // a set is dictionary<K, bool>
```

Equality is structural and built in (`==` compares structs memberwise), so there is no `PartialEq` to derive.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: `impl Display`, `operator<<`
text:
Write a `format` overload. `print`, `str` and `format` then render your type that way everywhere, including inside arrays and other structs.

```
struct Person { name: u8[..16], age: i32 }
fn format(out: u8[>..]&, p: Person) { format(out, p.name, " (", p.age, ")"); }

print(people);    // [ada (36), grace (45)]
```

Without an overload, everything still prints structurally (`Point { 1, 2 }`), which is often enough for debugging.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Ordering (`Ord`, `operator<`, comparators)
text:
Ordering comparisons (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`) exist on numbers only. Sorting takes a block that says "a goes before b":

```
sort(people) { a, b => a.age < b.age };
let oldest = max_by(people) { it.age };   // index of the largest
```

title: Operator overloading on math types

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Methods and `impl` blocks
text: There are none, but `x.f(a)` is exactly `f(x, a)` for every function, so method-call syntax works everywhere: `xs.sort()`, `d.insert(k, v)`, `2.5.describe()`. Group a type's functions in the same file or namespace as the type. There is also no namespace privacy in v1, so encapsulation is by convention.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Constructors
text: Struct literals do the job. Fields can declare defaults (evaluated per construction, may call functions), and ending a literal with `..` fills every unspecified field with its type's default. For invariants, write a plain `make_thing(...)` function that returns the struct; it is built in place at the caller.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Callbacks and closures: passed down, never stored
text: Function values in Goose are compile-time entities. You can pass a function or a block to another function, and every call through it is direct and inlinable. You cannot store one in a variable, a field or an array, and you cannot return one. There is no `std::function`, no `Box<dyn Fn>`, no function pointer.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Linked structures: nodes live in an array, links are references
text: Where C++ uses `unique_ptr<Node>` children and safe Rust gives up and uses `Vec<Node>` plus `u32` indices, Goose puts nodes in one grow-only array and links them with **typed references**. Because pushing never moves existing nodes, a reference you got from `push` stays valid forever, and the compiler checks it.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Self-relative vs pool-relative links
text:
| Form | Measured from | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `T&<u32>` | The field itself; target must be in the same array | The pool is a local or parameter, or you want to save/move the whole structure as bytes |
| `T&<u32 in pool>` | The base of the named global array `pool`, or of a global root struct's field such as `pool.items` | Other arrays need links into the pool, or you relink a lot |

A value holding self-relative links cannot be copied (the offsets would point elsewhere). Build it in place with `push` and bind it with `.=`.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Non-nested lifetimes: `shared_ptr` and `Rc` become pools
text:
Some data really does not die in stack order: cache entries, nodes of a graph being edited, open documents closed in any order, entities in a game. C++ reaches for `new`/`delete` or `shared_ptr`; Rust for `Rc<RefCell<T>>` or a slab crate. Goose's standard library gives you a **`slot_pool`**: a grow-only array, `items`, paired with a freelist. It is a root struct (see [Structs that own several vectors](#structs-that-own-several-vectors-a-root-struct)), so each pool is a local or global variable.

```
import slot_pool;

struct Item { id: i32, weight: f32 }
var pool = slot_pool<Item> {};

let s0 = pool.alloc_index(Item { 10, 1.0 });   // a slot index
let r  .= pool.alloc_ref(Item { 11, 1.0 });    // or a reference
pool.free(s0);                                 // slot 0 goes on the freelist
let s2 = pool.alloc_index(Item { 12, 2.0 });   // reuses slot 0
pool.free_ref(r);                              // a reference back to its slot
```

Read and iterate the elements through `pool.items`: `pool.items[s2]`, `for item in pool.items`. The language's older `reusable` and `reusable[]` pools are deprecated in favour of `slot_pool` and `slice_pool`.

**`free` releases nothing.** It puts an index on a freelist. Every slot stays a live, correctly typed value, so a stale reference to a reused slot reads a *different* `Item`, never garbage. That is a logic bug of the same class as a stale index into a `Vec`, not a use-after-free. Memory and type safety hold.

The practical rules that follow:

- Treat a freed slot like a stale index: stop using references to it after `free`. If you need to detect staleness, keep a generation counter in the element and compare it, as you would with a Rust slotmap key.
- The pool never shrinks; its high-water mark stays committed until the owning scope ends (or the program does, for a global). `pool.items.len` counts every slot ever appended, free ones included, and iterating `items` visits those too. `trim_memory()` in `os` returns pages above stack tops, not freed slots.
- Elements must be fixed-size. For variable-size data per slot, use the slice pool below.
- Ref-counting has no direct equivalent. Decide who owns the object (usually one place) and free it there; other holders keep references and accept the stale-slot semantics, or check a generation.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: When a pool is the wrong answer
text: Many "I need `shared_ptr`" cases are really "I need this to outlive the function that made it". Check first whether a caller's scope can own the data, with the callee pushing into an array passed down. That costs nothing and needs no freeing at all.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Structs that own several vectors: a root struct

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: What fits in an ordinary struct
text:
- Any number of fixed-size fields, including inline bounded arrays (`u8[..32]`, `Item[..8]`) and fixed-mode enums.
- Variable-size fields (`u8[]`, `T[varint]`) built once at construction.
- One growable tail: `struct Stack { name: u8[..8], items: i64[>..<] }`.

If your "vectors" have a real small bound, `T[..k]` keeps them inline and the struct stays fixed-size, so it can go in arrays too.

title: The context pattern

title: Recursion can't keep growable locals across the recursive call

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Updating a variable-size field
text: Fields like `u8[]` or `T[varint]`, and variable-mode enum values, are **frozen** once built. If a record's string needs to change, either give it a fixed-capacity field (`u8[..32]`, assignable) or rebuild the container. Fixed-size fields of the same record can be assigned freely.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Errors: three lightweight tools instead of `Result` or exceptions
text:
There is no `Result` type, no `?` operator and no unwinding exceptions. Goose gives you three tools, chosen by how far the error travels.

| Situation | C++ / Rust | Goose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two outcomes, caller handles it right away | `optional<T>`, `Result<T, E>` | A trailing `bool`: `-> T, bool` |
| Found or not | `T*` / `Option<&T>` | `T?`, a nullable reference into the input |
| Fails deep inside, handled far up | exceptions, `?` through every frame | `return E from f`, or the `exception` module |
| Bug or invariant | `assert`, `panic!` | `assert(c)`, `abort(msg)`, `exit(code)` |

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Trailing `bool`

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Optional references
text:
```
let big = xs.find() { it > 100 };   // T? into xs, null if none
if big { print(big); }               // narrowed: big is a T& inside
guard big else { return 0; }         // or: narrowed for the rest of the block
```

title: `return … from`: the long-distance return

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Typed `try`/`throw`

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Don't port `errno`-style or sentinel-heavy code
text: Indices use `-1` for "none" by library convention (`find`, `position`), which is fine. For anything richer, prefer the trailing `bool` or `T?` over magic values, because `T?` forces the caller to narrow before use.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: RAII and destructors: memory frees itself, everything else is explicit
text:
Goose has no destructors and no `Drop`. For memory you don't need them: scope exit resets the data stack, and since nothing inside Goose memory points to an external allocation, there is nothing to walk. Teardown of a million-element structure is one store.

What RAII also does in C++ and Rust is release *non-memory* resources: files, GPU buffers, sockets, locks. In Goose those are handles you release explicitly.

| Resource | C++ / Rust | Goose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File contents | `ifstream` closed by its destructor | `read_file(path, out)` / `write_file(path, data)`: whole-file calls, no handle to close |
| GPU buffer, texture, pipeline | Wrapper class with destructor | `gfx::Buffer { id }` handle; call `gfx::release(b)` |
| Physics world, body | Owning object | `physics::destroy(w)` |
| Mutex guard | `lock_guard`, `MutexGuard` | Not needed: threads share no memory |
| Scoped timer, "undo on exit" | Guard object | Do the work at the end of the block yourself |

Library handles carry a generation, so using one after release is reported as a misuse rather than a crash. A pattern that keeps release calls from drifting: create the handle in the function that owns its lifetime and release it at the end of that same function, as you would with a C API.

The standard library has **no `defer` or `finally`**. A cleanup callback can't be guaranteed to run on every exit, because a block's `return` or a `return … from` skips it. A design note proposes scope-exit cleanup; it is not implemented. Until then, put cleanup on each exit path, or structure the function so there is one exit.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Threads: no shared memory, only typed queues

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Serialization: your data is already a file format

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Smaller habits that change
text:
These trip people up in the first afternoon.

| Habit | In Goose |
| --- | --- |
| `cond ? a : b` | `if` is an expression: `let k = if hp > 50 { "ok" } else { "hurt" };` |
| Declare a variable, assign it in each branch | Use `if`/`match`/`block` as an expression, or `let n: i64;` assigned exactly once (checked) |
| Early-exit chains of `if (!x) return` | `guard x else { return; }`; inside `block { … }`, `break value` exits with a value |
| `let` / `const` meaning in Rust / C++ | `let` = can't reassign the name; contents still writable. `const T` = read-only contents. `var` = reassignable |
| `*p`, `p->x`, `&*p` | References are transparent: `p.x`. `.=` binds or rebinds, `.==` compares addresses |
| `std::tuple`, returning `(a, b)` | `-> A, B` and `let a, b = f();`. There is no tuple type, and an `if` branch can't yield `a, b` |
| `x++` in an expression | `++` and assignment are statements only |
| `if (n)` on an integer | Error: write `if n != 0`. `if` on an optional narrows it |
| `-7 % 3 == -1` | `%` is Euclidean: `-7 % 3 == 2`, always in `[0, abs(b))`. `rem` from `std` gives the C behaviour |
| Implicit promotion to `int` | Arithmetic runs at the operands' width; `u8 + u8` is 8-bit. `u32 + i32` is an error. Narrowing needs `as` (checked in debug) or `as!` (unchecked) |
| Signed overflow is UB / panics in debug | Aborts in debug, wraps in release. Unsigned always wraps |
| `for (auto& x : v) x *= 2;` | `for &x in xs { x *= 2; }`. Plain `for x in xs` gives a read-only copy for fixed-size elements |
| `printf("%d %s", …)` | `print("n=", n, " s=", s)`; `format_int` / `format_flt` for padding and precision |
| Labelled `break 'outer` | No labels in v1. Use a `block`, a nested function with `return`, or a flag |
| Recursion "just works" | Mark the cycle `recursive fn`, write full signatures, keep growable locals out of the recursive path |
| Separate compilation, `.so` plugins | Whole-program compilation to C. Goose libraries come as source packages (`goose build`) |

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: Bounds checks and speed
text: Every index is checked and the compiler removes the checks it can prove. Help it the way you'd help a vectorizer: one `assert` of the lengths at the top of a kernel lets it drop every check in the loop. `goose --bce-lines` shows which checks survived per line, and `checkfree fn` makes a surviving check a compile error. For `dist[adj[k]]`-style indirect indexing, index types (`u32 in nodes`) move the check to where the id is created.

docTitle: Goose for C++ and Rust programmers
title: What doesn't translate, and the nearest workaround
text:
Goose's speed and safety come from a closed world and static ownership. A few designs depend on exactly what it gives up.

| You want | Why it's not there | Nearest Goose shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runtime plugins, an open class hierarchy extended by other modules | No function pointers, no vtables, whole-program compilation | An enum of known kinds; for truly external code, C via `extern fn` / `extern "lib" { … }` |
| Closures stored in a struct or returned from a function | Function values must stay compile-time | Store an enum tag plus captured data; dispatch with case functions |
| `Vec<Vec<T>>` where each inner vector grows independently | An array element can't be resizable | Runs from a `slice_pool<T>`, a flat array plus offsets, or `T[..k]` rows if bounded |
| Random access into an array of variable-size records | Offsets depend on every earlier element | Fixed-size elements with inline capacity, or an index array of references beside it |
| Taking a reference into a fixed-mode enum payload | It could be overwritten with another variant | Store it in variable mode (`T..`), or copy, modify and reassign |
| Changing the variant of a packed (`T..`) element | Its neighbours are packed right behind it | Fixed mode, or rebuild the container |
| `shared_ptr` with automatic last-owner cleanup | No refcounts, no destructors | Pick an owner; `slot_pool` + explicit `free`; generation field to detect staleness |
| Shared mutable state between threads | No shared memory by design | Messages through typed queues |
| An array of objects that each own several growable members | A root struct must be a local or global variable | One root struct holding a field per member, with slot indices or a `slice_pool` for the per-object parts |
| Subprocesses, networking | Not in the v1 library | `extern fn` to C |

As a rule of thumb, when something won't compile, read the whole error. It names both ends, such as the reference and where it was bound, or the holder and the line that stored into it, which usually tells you which scope or binding to move.

title: Goose in other editors
text:
The compiler is its own language server: `goose lsp` speaks the Language
Server Protocol on stdin and stdout, so any editor with an LSP client can
use it. VS Code has an [extension](../vscode/README.md) that starts it for
you. For Neovim, Helix and Emacs, the configuration below is all that is
needed.

Every snippet starts `goose lsp` assuming the compiler is on PATH; if it
is not, replace `goose` with the executable's full path. The server finds
the standard library the way `goose check` does (`GOOSE_STDLIB`, or the
`stdlib/` directory near the executable). For a compiler that is not in
its source checkout, add `--stdlib` and the directory to the command:
`goose lsp --stdlib /path/to/goose/stdlib`.

Each open file is analyzed as a program of its own, with the files it
imports. To have a module checked as part of the program that imports it
(and the errors of that program shown in it), name the program's entry
file in the client's initialization options, as an absolute path:
`{ "entryFiles": ["/path/to/project/main.goose"] }`. The snippets show
where these options go.

The server's semantic tokens color names by what they resolve to
(functions, types, fields, variants, parameters, variables). They do not
cover keywords, strings or comments, and the TextMate grammar is only part
of the VS Code extension.

title: Neovim
text:
Neovim 0.11 or later, in `init.lua`:

```lua
vim.filetype.add({ extension = { goose = 'goose' } })
vim.lsp.config('goose', {
  cmd = { 'goose', 'lsp' },
  filetypes = { 'goose' },
  root_markers = { '.git' },
  -- init_options = { entryFiles = { '/path/to/project/main.goose' } },
})
vim.lsp.enable('goose')
```

On Neovim 0.10, start it from the filetype instead:

```lua
vim.filetype.add({ extension = { goose = 'goose' } })
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('FileType', {
  pattern = 'goose',
  callback = function(ev)
    vim.lsp.start({ name = 'goose', cmd = { 'goose', 'lsp' }, root_dir = vim.fs.root(ev.buf, { '.git' }) })
  end,
})
```

By default, Neovim shows diagnostics, hover (`K`), go to definition
(`CTRL-]`), references (`grr`), rename (`grn`), document symbols (`gO`),
signature help (`CTRL-S` in Insert mode), completion (`CTRL-X CTRL-O`, or
as you type with `vim.lsp.completion.enable`) and semantic highlighting.
Inlay hints need `vim.lsp.inlay_hint.enable()`, folding needs
`foldmethod=expr` and `foldexpr=v:lua.vim.lsp.foldexpr()`, and code lenses
need `vim.lsp.codelens.refresh()` (called on `BufEnter` and `InsertLeave`,
for example). The lenses above generic functions count their
instantiations. To list the instantiations with `vim.lsp.codelens.run()`,
give Neovim the command and tell the server that the client has it:

```lua
vim.lsp.commands['goose.showInstantiations'] = function(command)
  vim.ui.select(command.arguments[2], { prompt = 'Instantiations of ' .. command.arguments[1] }, function() end)
end
-- and in vim.lsp.config('goose', ...):
--   init_options = { commands = { 'goose.showInstantiations' } },
```

title: Helix
text:
In `languages.toml` (in Helix's configuration directory, or `.helix/` in
the project):

```toml
[language-server.goose]
command = "goose"
args = ["lsp"]

title: config = { entryFiles = ["/path/to/project/main.goose"] }
text:
[[language]]
name = "goose"
scope = "source.goose"
file-types = ["goose"]
roots = [".git"]
comment-token = "//"
indent = { tab-width = 4, unit = "    " }
language-servers = ["goose"]
```

(`config` is what Helix sends as the initialization options.)

Helix shows diagnostics, hover (`space k`), go to definition (`gd`),
references (`gr`), rename (`space r`), document and workspace symbols
(`space s`, `space S`), signature help and completion as you type, and
inlay hints with `display-inlay-hints = true` under `[editor.lsp]` in
`config.toml`. Helix highlights with tree-sitter grammars, and Goose has
none. Helix also has no semantic tokens, folding or code lenses, so Goose
files are shown without colors.

title: Emacs
text:
With Eglot (built in since Emacs 29), in `init.el`:

```elisp
(define-derived-mode goose-mode prog-mode "Goose"
  (setq-local comment-start "// "))
(add-to-list 'auto-mode-alist '("\\.goose\\'" . goose-mode))
(with-eval-after-load 'eglot
  (add-to-list 'eglot-server-programs '(goose-mode "goose" "lsp")))
(add-hook 'goose-mode-hook #'eglot-ensure)
```

For entry files, the server program takes the options after the command:
`'(goose-mode "goose" "lsp" :initializationOptions (:entryFiles ["/path/to/project/main.goose"]))`.

Eglot shows diagnostics through Flymake, hover and signature help in
ElDoc, go to definition (`M-.`), references (`M-?`), rename
(`eglot-rename`), document symbols in Imenu, workspace symbols
(`xref-find-apropos`), completion (`completion-at-point`) and inlay hints;
the newest Eglot, from GNU ELPA, highlights with semantic tokens too
(`eglot-semantic-tokens-mode`). Eglot has no folding or code lenses.

title: Formatting
text:
`goose format` rewrites files in the standard layout: indentation, the
spaces between tokens, blank lines and trailing commas, with the line
breaks left where they are. As with gofmt, the types and `=`s of a run of
declarations (consecutive `const`s, a struct's fields) line up in columns. It takes files and directories (a directory
stands for the `.goose` files under it), and with none, or `-`, formats
standard input to standard output. A file that does not parse is left as
it is and its errors printed, with exit status 2; `goose format --check`
writes nothing and lists the files that are not formatted, with exit
status 1, for a CI step or a commit hook.

The language server formats too (`textDocument/formatting`), the editor's
text rather than the file on disk, with edits to the lines that change
only, so the cursor and marks on the others stay. A document that does not
parse gets no edits; its diagnostics say why.

In Neovim, `vim.lsp.buf.format()` formats; to format on save, in the
configuration above:

```lua
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('BufWritePre', {
  pattern = '*.goose',
  callback = function() vim.lsp.buf.format() end,
})
```

In Helix, `:format` formats, and `auto-format = true` in the `[[language]]`
entry above formats on save.

In Emacs, `eglot-format-buffer` formats; to format on save:

```elisp
(add-hook 'goose-mode-hook
          (lambda () (add-hook 'before-save-hook #'eglot-format-buffer nil t)))
```

Without the language server, an editor can run `goose format -` on the
buffer instead: with [conform.nvim](https://github.com/stevearc/conform.nvim)
in Neovim, say,

```lua
require('conform').setup({
  formatters = { goose = { command = 'goose', args = { 'format', '-' }, stdin = true } },
  formatters_by_ft = { goose = { 'goose' } },
  format_on_save = { timeout_ms = 2000 },
})
```

or `formatter = { command = "goose", args = ["format", "-"] }` in Helix's
`[[language]]` entry.
